lessons.title: The Digestive System — Organs and Their Order
lessons.notes_html:
The Digestive Tract

Digestion starts in the mouth and ends at the anus. The tube through which food passes is called the digestive tract (alimentary canal). Food moves through it in this order:

OrderOrganWhat happens there
1MouthTeeth chew the food; saliva starts changing starch
2OesophagusThe food pipe that pushes food down to the stomach
3StomachGastric juice starts digesting protein; food is mixed and softened
4Small intestineDigestion is completed and digested food is absorbed into the blood
5Large intestine, rectum, anusWater is absorbed and waste leaves the body

Accessory Organs: Liver and Pancreas

The liver and the pancreas are NOT part of the digestive tract, because food does not pass through them. They are accessory organs — they only send their juices into the tract.

  • The liver makes bile, a greenish juice that goes into the small intestine and breaks fat into small droplets.
  • The pancreas sends pancreatic juice into the small intestine.
  • The gallbladder is a small green sac below the liver.

The Epiglottis — A Safety Flap

The epiglottis is a small flap that closes the windpipe during swallowing, so food cannot enter the windpipe. This is why we should not talk while eating: while talking, the windpipe passage stays open and a piece of food may go into it, causing coughing or choking.

mcqs.q: Which juice comes out of the liver?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: Bile. Bile is a greenish juice made by the liver. It goes into the small intestine and breaks fat into small droplets, so remember: liver → bile.

mcqs.q: Which is the correct order of the organs of the digestive tract?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: Mouth ← Oesophagus ← Stomach ← Small intestine. Food is chewed in the mouth, pushed down the oesophagus, mixed in the stomach, and then passes into the small intestine.

mcqs.q: Which organ stops food from entering the windpipe while eating?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: Epiglottis. The epiglottis is a small flap that closes the windpipe during swallowing, so food goes down the food pipe and not into the windpipe.

mcqs.q: Why are the liver and the pancreas not counted as part of the digestive tract?
options: Food does not pass through them; they only send juices into the tract
They do not make any juice
mcqs.why: Correct answer: food does not pass through them. The liver and pancreas are accessory organs — they help digestion by sending juices (bile and pancreatic juice) into the digestive tract, but food never enters them.

mcqs.q: Why should we not talk while eating?
options: While talking the windpipe stays open and food may enter it, causing choking
mcqs.why: Correct answer: while talking, the passage of the windpipe stays open, so a piece of food may slip into the windpipe and cause coughing or choking. During swallowing, the epiglottis normally closes the windpipe.

mcqs.q: In a diagram of the digestive system, where is the pancreas found?
options: At the end of the large intestine
mcqs.why: Correct answer: below and behind the stomach. The pancreas is a long, thin organ lying below and behind the stomach; the liver is the large reddish organ at the upper right of the stomach, with the gallbladder below it.

mcqs.q: What is the gallbladder?
options: A small green sac below the liver
The last part of the intestine
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the gallbladder is a small green sac found below the liver. In the digestive system diagram it is drawn under the liver, near the stomach.

mcqs.q: Which of these organs does food actually pass through?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the stomach. Food passes through the mouth, oesophagus, stomach and intestines. The liver, pancreas and gallbladder are accessory parts — food does not pass through them.

mcqs.q: Bile helps digestion by:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: bile breaks fat into small droplets. This happens in the small intestine, and then the pancreatic juice enzymes can digest the fat easily.

mcqs.q: The long tube that carries food from the mouth to the stomach is the:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the oesophagus. It is the food pipe between the mouth (pharynx) and the stomach; the windpipe is the air passage beside it.

lessons.title: How Digestion Works — Physical and Chemical Digestion
lessons.notes_html:
Two Kinds of Digestion

Physical (mechanical) digestionChemical digestion
Food is broken into small pieces with no chemical changeFood is changed into new, simpler substances by enzymes
In the mouth: teeth chew the food. In the stomach: muscular walls make mixing waves that mix food with gastric juice and soften itEnzymes break large molecules into smaller molecules, e.g. starch into sugar

What Enzymes Do

Enzymes speed up chemical processes and break large food molecules into smaller molecules so that food can be digested and absorbed. For example, the salivary enzyme changes starch into glucose.

Digestion of a Fried Potato (Starch + Fat), Step by Step

  • Mouth: the salivary enzyme starts changing starch into glucose. Word equation: Starch + salivary enzyme → Glucose. Fat is not digested here.
  • Stomach: no chemical digestion of starch or fat takes place. The gastric juice only kills germs and starts the digestion of protein (protein digestion begins in the stomach and finishes in the small intestine).
  • Small intestine: bile breaks fat into small droplets; pancreatic juice enzymes change starch into sugar and fat into fatty acids and glycerol. Word equations: Starch + pancreatic enzyme → Sugar; Fat + bile + pancreatic enzyme → Fatty acids + Glycerol.

Why Fat Is Not Digested in the Mouth or Stomach

Neither saliva nor gastric juice can break down fat. Fat is first broken into droplets by bile and then digested in the small intestine by pancreatic juice enzymes.

Absorption — Only in the Small Intestine

Absorption of digested food takes place only in the small intestine, because its walls have tiny projections called villi with blood capillaries. Through the villi, digested food passes into the blood. No other organ has this structure.

mcqs.q: In which organ does the chemical digestion of protein begin?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: in the stomach. The gastric juice of the stomach starts the chemical digestion of protein; it is completed in the small intestine, where protein is changed into amino acids.

mcqs.q: Physical (mechanical) digestion means:
options: Changing food into new substances with enzymes
Breaking food into small pieces without any chemical change
mcqs.why: Correct answer: breaking food into small pieces without any chemical change. The teeth chew food in the mouth, and the stomach walls make mixing waves — the food stays the same substance, only smaller and softer.

mcqs.q: What happens to food in the stomach during physical digestion?
options: It is absorbed into the blood
Muscular walls make mixing waves that mix it with gastric juice and soften it
It is changed into amino acids
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the stomach's muscular walls make mixing waves that mix the food with gastric juice and soften it. This is physical digestion — no new substance is formed.

mcqs.q: The main work of enzymes is to:
options: Speed up chemical processes and break large molecules into smaller ones
Kill all germs in the body
mcqs.why: Correct answer: enzymes speed up chemical processes and break large molecules into smaller molecules so food can be digested — for example, the salivary enzyme changes starch into glucose.

mcqs.q: Why are fatty foods not digested in the mouth or the stomach?
options: Fat is too heavy to move
Fat dissolves in water too quickly
The mouth and stomach are too cold
Neither saliva nor gastric juice breaks down fat
mcqs.why: Correct answer: neither the saliva nor the gastric juice breaks down fat. Fat is broken into droplets by bile and digested in the small intestine by pancreatic juice enzymes.

mcqs.q: In the mouth, the salivary enzyme starts changing:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: starch into glucose. The word equation is: Starch + salivary enzyme → Glucose. This is the first step of chemical digestion, in the mouth.

mcqs.q: In the small intestine, fat is finally changed into:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: fatty acids and glycerol. First bile breaks the fat into small droplets, then pancreatic enzymes complete the change: Fat + bile + pancreatic enzyme → Fatty acids + Glycerol.

mcqs.q: Why does absorption of food take place only in the small intestine?
options: Its walls have villi and blood capillaries that absorb digested food into the blood
It receives bile from the liver
mcqs.why: Correct answer: its walls have tiny projections (villi) with blood capillaries, through which digested food is absorbed into the blood. No other organ of the tract has this structure.

mcqs.q: What does the gastric juice do in the stomach?
options: Kills germs and starts protein digestion
mcqs.why: Correct answer: gastric juice kills germs in the food and starts the chemical digestion of protein. It does not digest starch or fat.

mcqs.q: The tiny finger-like projections on the wall of the small intestine are called:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: villi. The villi greatly help absorption: digested food passes through them into the blood capillaries and is carried to the whole body.

lessons.title: Breathing, Respiration and Gaseous Exchange
lessons.notes_html:
Breathing and Respiration Are Different

BreathingRespiration
A physical process — air only moves in and outA chemical process inside the cells
No chemical change takes place and no enzyme takes partEnergy is released from glucose and oxygen
Energy is used up in breathingEnergy is produced and released in respiration

Why Breathing Is a Physical Process

In breathing, air only moves in and out of the lungs. No chemical change takes place and no enzyme takes part, so breathing is a physical process.

Gaseous Exchange in the Lungs

The lungs contain tiny air sacs called alveoli, wrapped in blood capillaries. In gaseous exchange:

  • Oxygen from the air in the alveoli passes into the blood capillaries.
  • Carbon dioxide from the blood passes into the air of the alveoli and is breathed out.

The blood capillary around the alveolus carries the oxygen away to the body (oxygenated blood) and brings carbon-dioxide-rich blood (deoxygenated blood) to the lungs.

mcqs.q: Which row gives the correct difference between breathing and respiration?
options: Breathing needs oxygen, respiration does not
In breathing energy is used up, in respiration energy is released
Carbon dioxide is breathed out in breathing but not in respiration
In breathing air goes in, in respiration air goes out
mcqs.why: Correct answer: in breathing energy is used up, in respiration energy is released. Breathing is a physical process that needs energy; respiration is a chemical process in which energy is produced from glucose and oxygen.

mcqs.q: Why is the act of breathing a physical process?
options: Because air only moves in and out — no chemical change and no enzyme takes part
Because it happens in the lungs
mcqs.why: Correct answer: in breathing, air only moves in and out; there is no chemical change and no enzyme takes part. That is why breathing is physical, while respiration (which releases energy) is chemical.

mcqs.q: Gaseous exchange takes place in the lungs between the blood and:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the alveoli. Oxygen from the air in the alveoli passes into the blood capillaries, and carbon dioxide from the blood passes into the alveoli to be breathed out.

mcqs.q: During gaseous exchange, oxygen moves:
options: From the blood into the alveoli
From the stomach into the blood
From the blood into the stomach
From the alveoli into the blood capillaries
mcqs.why: Correct answer: from the alveoli into the blood. The air in the alveoli is rich in oxygen, so oxygen passes into the blood, making it oxygenated blood.

mcqs.q: During gaseous exchange, carbon dioxide moves:
options: From the alveoli into the blood
From the air into the lungs only
From the blood into the alveoli, and is then breathed out
From the food into the blood
mcqs.why: Correct answer: carbon dioxide passes from the blood capillaries into the air of the alveoli, and it is then breathed out of the body.

mcqs.q: Respiration is a chemical process because:
options: Energy is released from glucose and oxygen in a chemical change
mcqs.why: Correct answer: in respiration, glucose and oxygen take part in a chemical change and energy is produced and released. No such chemical change happens in simple breathing.

mcqs.q: The tiny air sacs of the lungs are surrounded by:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: blood capillaries. The thin walls of the alveoli and capillaries let oxygen and carbon dioxide pass between the air and the blood.

mcqs.q: Blood that has just received oxygen in the lungs is called:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: oxygenated blood. Blood leaving the alveoli is rich in oxygen; blood arriving there is deoxygenated (rich in carbon dioxide).

mcqs.q: Which of these is NOT part of gaseous exchange?
options: Digested food enters the blood through villi
Air is breathed out of the lungs
mcqs.why: Correct answer: digested food entering the blood happens in the small intestine through villi — that is absorption, not gaseous exchange. Gaseous exchange is only about oxygen and carbon dioxide in the lungs.

mcqs.q: Breathing can be observed in animals because:
options: A living animal in an airtight bottle shows signs of breathing and stays alive
mcqs.why: Correct answer: in the book's experiment, the living cockroach in the airtight bottle stayed alive and showed signs of breathing, while the dead one showed no activity — proving that animals breathe.

lessons.title: Keeping the Respiratory System Healthy
lessons.notes_html:
How Polluted Air Harms Us

Polluted air contains dust, smoke and germs. These damage the respiratory system and cause diseases like cold, asthma and cough.

Steps to Avoid Diseases of the Respiratory System

  • Eat fresh fruits and vegetables.
  • Exercise regularly.
  • Live in a clean environment.
  • Avoid pollution.
  • Get proper vaccination.
  • Avoid smoking.

The Breathing Experiment (Project)

In the book's project, a living cockroach and a dead cockroach were kept in separate airtight conical flasks:

  • The living cockroach stayed alive and showed signs of breathing; the dead one showed no activity. This proves that animals breathe.
  • A small animal like a cockroach was chosen because it fits easily into the flask and its breathing can be observed easily.
  • The flasks were airtight so that outside air could not enter — any change in the air inside was only because of the animal's breathing.

mcqs.q: Why does polluted air cause diseases of breathing?
options: Its dust, smoke and germs damage the respiratory system
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the dust, smoke and germs in polluted air damage the respiratory system, causing diseases like cold, asthma and cough. Clean air keeps the lungs healthy.

mcqs.q: Which of these diseases is a disease of the respiratory system?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: asthma. Asthma, cold and cough are breathing diseases caused or made worse by polluted air; the others are not diseases of the respiratory system.

mcqs.q: Which habit must be avoided to keep the respiratory system healthy?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: smoking. The book's steps for a healthy respiratory system include eating fresh fruits and vegetables, regular exercise and proper vaccination — and avoiding smoking and pollution.

mcqs.q: In the breathing experiment, why were airtight conical flasks used?
options: So outside air could not enter and any change was only due to the animal's breathing
To stop the cockroach escaping only
To make the flask look clear
mcqs.why: Correct answer: airtight flasks stop outside air from entering, so any change in the air inside the bottle is only because of the animal's breathing — that makes the experiment fair.

mcqs.q: Why was a cockroach used as the specimen animal in the experiment?
options: It is the only animal that breathes
It lives without food for years
It is small, fits easily in the flask, and its breathing is easy to observe
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the cockroach is a small animal that fits easily into the conical flask, and its breathing can easily be observed during the experiment.

mcqs.q: What was observed in the flask with the living cockroach?
options: It stayed alive and showed signs of breathing
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the living cockroach stayed alive and showed signs of breathing, while in the bottle with the dead cockroach no such activity was seen — this proves that animals breathe.

mcqs.q: Which step helps protect the respiratory system?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: proper vaccination. Together with fresh food, regular exercise, a clean environment and avoiding pollution and smoking, vaccination protects us from breathing diseases.

mcqs.q: Fresh fruits and vegetables help the respiratory system by:
options: Keeping the body strong against diseases
mcqs.why: Correct answer: fresh fruits and vegetables are part of the book's steps to avoid respiratory diseases — a healthy diet keeps the body and its breathing system strong.

mcqs.q: A clean environment protects us because:
options: Its air has less dust, smoke and germs to damage the lungs
mcqs.why: Correct answer: clean air contains little dust, smoke and germs, so the respiratory system is not damaged and diseases like cold, asthma and cough are avoided.

mcqs.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
options: Cough — disease of the respiratory system
mcqs.why: Correct answer: cough is a disease of the respiratory system, like cold and asthma. Smoking is a harmful habit that damages this system and must be avoided.

lessons.title: The Heart and the Flow of Blood
lessons.notes_html:
The Four Chambers of the Heart

ChamberPositionWork
Right atriumUpper rightReceives deoxygenated blood from the body
Left atriumUpper leftReceives oxygenated blood from the lungs
Right ventricleLower rightPumps blood to the lungs
Left ventricleLower leftPumps blood to the whole body

The atria (upper chambers) only receive blood, so their walls are thin. The ventricles (lower chambers) must push blood out with force, so their walls are thick — the left ventricle's wall is thickest of all because it pumps blood to the whole body.

The Path of Blood Through the Heart

Body → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body.

  • Deoxygenated blood from the body reaches the right atrium of the heart.
  • It goes from the heart to the lungs through the pulmonary artery.
  • The aorta is the great artery that carries blood to the whole body.
  • Valves in the heart (tricuspid, bicuspid/mitral, pulmonary and aortic valves) stop blood flowing backwards.

Oxygenated and Deoxygenated Blood

Oxygenated bloodDeoxygenated blood
More oxygen, less carbon dioxideLess oxygen, more carbon dioxide
Goes from the lungs to the heart and the bodyGoes from the body to the heart and the lungs

mcqs.q: Deoxygenated blood from the body reaches which part of the heart first?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the right atrium. Deoxygenated blood from the body enters the right atrium (the right upper chamber) through the vena cava, then passes to the right ventricle.

mcqs.q: Deoxygenated blood goes from the heart to the lungs through the:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the pulmonary artery. It is the only artery that carries deoxygenated blood — from the right ventricle to the lungs, where the blood picks up oxygen.

mcqs.q: Which vessel carries blood from the heart to the whole body?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the aorta. The aorta is the largest artery; it receives oxygenated blood from the left ventricle and carries it to the whole body.

mcqs.q: Why are the walls of the ventricles thicker than the walls of the atria?
options: Ventricles must push blood out with force, while atria only receive blood
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the ventricles push blood out with force — the right ventricle to the lungs and the left ventricle to the whole body — so their walls are thick and muscular; the atria only receive blood, so their walls are thin.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between atria and ventricles?
options: Atria are lower, ventricles are upper
Atria are the upper chambers that receive blood with thin walls; ventricles are the lower chambers that pump blood out with thick walls
Atria carry blood to the lungs only
mcqs.why: Correct answer: atria are the two upper, thin-walled receiving chambers; ventricles are the two lower, thick-walled pumping chambers. This structure matches their different jobs.

mcqs.q: Oxygenated blood is blood that:
options: Has more oxygen and less carbon dioxide
Has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide
mcqs.why: Correct answer: oxygenated blood has more oxygen and less carbon dioxide. It goes from the lungs to the heart and then to the body; deoxygenated blood has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide.

mcqs.q: Oxygenated blood returns from the lungs to the heart through the:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the pulmonary vein. It brings oxygen-rich blood from the lungs into the left atrium — it is the exception among veins, which usually carry deoxygenated blood.

mcqs.q: Which chamber pumps blood to the whole body?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the left ventricle. It pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta for the whole body, which is why its wall is the thickest of all four chambers.

mcqs.q: In the heart diagram, the blood flow is correctly shown as:
options: Right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → left atrium
mcqs.why: Correct answer: right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium. Blood goes to the lungs to pick up oxygen, then returns to the left side of the heart.

mcqs.q: The valves inside the heart are needed to:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: valves (tricuspid, bicuspid/mitral, pulmonary and aortic) let blood flow in one direction only and stop it from flowing backwards between the chambers.

lessons.title: Blood Vessels — Arteries and Veins
lessons.notes_html:
Arteries and Veins Compared

ArteriesVeins
Carry blood from the heart to the bodyBring blood back from the body to the heart
Walls are thick and muscularWalls are thin
Blood pressure is highBlood pressure is low
No valvesValves present to stop back-flow

Why Veins Have Valves

The blood pressure in veins is low, and blood has to travel back to the heart (often upwards, against gravity). The valves stop the blood from flowing backwards and let it flow only towards the heart.

The Two Exceptions

  • Almost all arteries carry oxygen-rich blood — except the pulmonary artery, which carries deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs.
  • The pulmonary veins are the opposite exception: they carry oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart.

mcqs.q: Why are there valves in the veins?
options: Blood pressure in veins is low, so valves stop blood flowing backwards and let it flow only towards the heart
mcqs.why: Correct answer: veins have low blood pressure, so without valves the returning blood could flow backwards. The valves keep it moving in one direction — towards the heart.

mcqs.q: Why is there oxygen-rich blood in all arteries except the pulmonary artery?
options: All arteries carry blood from the heart to the body, but the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs to collect oxygen
The pulmonary artery is not an artery
Oxygen enters arteries from the air
mcqs.why: Correct answer: arteries carry blood away from the heart to the body, so they carry oxygen-rich blood — except the pulmonary artery, whose job is to take deoxygenated blood to the lungs.

mcqs.q: Which statement about arteries is correct?
options: They have thin walls and valves
They bring blood back to the heart
They carry blood to the body, have thick muscular walls, high pressure and no valves
mcqs.why: Correct answer: arteries carry blood from the heart to the body; their walls are thick and muscular, the pressure in them is high, and they have no valves.

mcqs.q: Which statement about veins is correct?
options: They have thick walls and high pressure
They bring blood back to the heart, have thin walls, low pressure and valves
They carry blood only to the lungs
mcqs.why: Correct answer: veins bring blood back from the body to the heart; their walls are thin, pressure is low, and they have valves to stop back-flow.

mcqs.q: The pulmonary veins are special because they:
options: Carry deoxygenated blood like all veins
Carry oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium. Together with the pulmonary artery, they are the two exceptions to the usual artery/vein rule.

mcqs.q: Blood pressure is high in:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: arteries. The heart pumps blood directly into the arteries with force, so their pressure is high and their walls are thick and muscular.

mcqs.q: If a vein had no valves, the blood in it could:
options: Flow backwards, away from the heart
mcqs.why: Correct answer: it could flow backwards. Because pressure in veins is low, valves are needed to make sure blood flows only towards the heart.

mcqs.q: Which vessel carries blood to the whole body?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the aorta. In the book's matching exercise, 'carries blood to the whole body' matches the aorta — the great artery leaving the left ventricle.

mcqs.q: Arteries and veins both:
options: Carry blood only to the heart
mcqs.why: Correct answer: both are blood vessels that carry blood through the body. They differ in direction, wall thickness, pressure and the presence of valves.

mcqs.q: The blood in the pulmonary artery is:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: deoxygenated blood going to the lungs. The right ventricle pumps it through the pulmonary artery so it can pick up oxygen in the lungs.

lessons.title: Heart Diseases and Organ Replacement
lessons.notes_html:
Blood Pressure and Hypertension

The heart's pumping also produces blood pressure. When the blood pressure becomes too high, the condition is called high blood pressure (hypertension).

Heart Attack — A Blockage Problem

  • Cholesterol and fatty substances collect in the walls of the arteries and make them narrow.
  • The blood supply to the heart muscles is reduced or stopped.
  • The part of the heart that gets no blood starts dying — this is a heart attack.

So a heart attack is caused by blockage in the arteries that supply the heart itself.

Transplantation

Replacing a damaged organ of the body with a healthy organ is called transplantation. A healthy heart, kidney or other organ from a donor can be placed in a patient whose own organ is damaged, so that transport and other body systems keep working.

mcqs.q: High blood pressure is also called:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: hypertension. In the book's matching exercise, 'also produces blood pressure' leads to high blood pressure — hypertension — when the pressure rises too much.

mcqs.q: A heart attack is caused by:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: blockage in the arteries. Cholesterol and fatty substances collect in the artery walls, narrow them, and stop the blood supply to the heart muscles.

mcqs.q: Why does a heart attack happen when the arteries narrow?
options: The blood supply to the heart muscles stops and that part of the heart starts dying
mcqs.why: Correct answer: when fatty substances narrow the arteries, the heart muscles do not receive enough blood, and the starved part of the heart starts dying — that is a heart attack.

mcqs.q: Which substances collect in artery walls and narrow them?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: cholesterol and fatty substances. They build up inside the walls of the arteries over time, making the passage narrow and reducing blood flow.

mcqs.q: Replacing a damaged organ of the body with a healthy organ is called:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: transplantation. A damaged organ (for example a heart or kidney) is replaced with a healthy organ so the body can keep working.

mcqs.q: The part of the heart in a heart attack starts dying because:
options: It does not receive blood through the narrowed arteries
mcqs.why: Correct answer: it does not receive blood. The heart muscles need their own blood supply; when narrowed arteries block it, that part of the heart is starved and begins to die.

mcqs.q: Blood pressure is produced by:
options: The pumping action of the heart
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the pumping of the heart produces blood pressure, which pushes blood through the arteries to the whole body.

mcqs.q: Which of these can narrow the arteries?
options: Fatty substances collecting in their walls
mcqs.why: Correct answer: fatty substances (with cholesterol) collecting in the artery walls narrow them. This narrowing is the root cause of a heart attack in this chapter.

mcqs.q: A healthy organ taken from a donor is used in:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: transplantation — replacing a patient's damaged organ with a healthy one so that the body's transport system and other functions continue.

mcqs.q: Hypertension means:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: hypertension is high blood pressure. It is matched in the book's exercise with the heart's pumping, which produces blood pressure.

lessons.title: Transport in Plants — Xylem and Phloem
lessons.notes_html:
How Water Enters and Rises in a Plant

  • Root hairs absorb water (and minerals) from the soil.
  • The water travels up through long tubes called xylem vessels to the roots, stem and leaves.
  • The force that pulls water from the roots up to the leaf cells is called the transpiration pull (with help from root pressure).

Xylem and Phloem — Two Transport Tissues

XylemPhloem
Carries water (and minerals) from roots to stem and leavesCarries food from the leaves to all parts of the plant
Made of dead, hollow, continuous vessels; flow is one way — roots → leavesFood moves to where it is needed, above and below the leaves

The Ringing Experiment (Project)

A ring of outer bark together with the phloem was cut away from a stem, while the inner wood (xylem) was left intact:

  • The part above the cut swelled up, because food coming down from the leaves collected there.
  • The part below the cut became weak and wilted, because food could not reach it.
  • The plant that was not cut showed no such change.
  • Conclusion: the phloem transports food in the plant; when the phloem path is cut, food does not reach below and collects above the cut.

Note on direction: the book explains that water rises through the xylem in one direction — from the roots to the stem and leaves — because of root pressure and the transpiration pull.

mcqs.q: Water is absorbed from the soil by the:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: root hairs. In the book's matching exercise, 'absorb water from the soil' matches root hairs — tiny hair-like parts of the roots.

mcqs.q: Which tissue carries water in plants?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: xylem. The xylem vessels are long tubes that carry water from the roots to the stem and leaves.

mcqs.q: The force that pulls water from the roots to the leaf cells is called:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the transpiration pull. As water evaporates from the leaves, it pulls more water up through the xylem from the roots (root pressure also helps).

mcqs.q: The long tubes that carry water to the roots, stem and leaves are called:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: xylem vessels. They are dead, hollow and continuous tubes running from the roots through the stem to the leaves.

mcqs.q: The phloem's job in a plant is to:
options: Carry food from the leaves to other parts of the plant
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the phloem transports food made in the leaves to the other parts of the plant — above and below the leaves.

mcqs.q: In the ringing experiment, which tissues were cut and removed?
options: The ring of outer bark together with the phloem, while the xylem was left intact
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the outer bark ring with the phloem was cut away and the inner wood (xylem) was left intact — so any change seen must be due to the missing phloem.

mcqs.q: What was seen at the cut part of the plant?
options: The part above the cut swelled up because food collected there
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the part above the cut ring swelled (bulged), because the food coming from the leaves could not pass the cut and collected above it.

mcqs.q: What effect did the cut have on the lower part of the plant?
options: It became weak and wilted because food could not reach it
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the lower part became weak and wilted, because the cut blocked the phloem path and food from the leaves could not reach below the cut.

mcqs.q: The conclusion of the ringing experiment is:
options: Phloem transports food in the plant; when its path is cut, food collects above the cut and does not reach below
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the phloem transports food in the plant. When the phloem path is cut, food does not reach below and collects above the cut — exactly what the swelling showed.

mcqs.q: Water rises through the xylem:
options: In one direction — from the roots to the stem and leaves
mcqs.why: Correct answer: in one direction, from the roots to the leaves. The book explains this rise is due to root pressure and the transpiration pull through the dead, hollow xylem vessels.

chapters.title: Environment and Its Effects on Living Things

lessons.title: Habitats and Their Kinds
lessons.notes_html:
What Is a Habitat?

A habitat is the environmental region in which an organism lives, and where it gets food, shelter, protection and facilities to reproduce. The living of an organism in a particular environment is called its habitat. Every habitat has its own special conditions of temperature, light, moisture, soil and water.

The Two Main Kinds of Habitats

Aquatic (water) habitatsFeatures
Fresh-waterRivers, streams and ponds
Sea-waterSea and salty water
EstuarineWhere the river meets the sea; the water there is brackish — neither fully fresh nor fully salty
Terrestrial (land) habitatsFeatures
ForestHeavy rain, dense trees
GrasslandGrassy plains
DesertVery little rain, hot and dry
TundraCovered with snow, very cold

Animals of Water Habitats

The organs of animals living in water are made according to the water environment: they obtain oxygen and food from the water itself, their bodies are made to swim and move in water, and some animals, like whales and sharks, live only in water.

mcqs.q: What is a habitat?
options: A group of the same species
The environmental region where an organism lives and gets food, shelter, protection and facilities to reproduce
A chain of animals eating each other
mcqs.why: Correct answer: a habitat is the environmental region in which an organism lives and where it gets food, shelter, protection and facilities to reproduce — for example, a pond for a fish or a desert for a camel.

mcqs.q: The living of an organism in a particular environment is called its:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: habitat. The habitat is the particular environment — with its own temperature, light, moisture, soil and water — in which an organism lives.

mcqs.q: The water of the area where the river meets the sea is called:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: brackish water. In the estuarine habitat, the fresh water of the river mixes with the salty water of the sea, so the water is neither fully fresh nor fully salty.

mcqs.q: A cold region covered with snow is called:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: tundra. Tundra is a very cold terrestrial habitat covered with snow, where living is very difficult for organisms.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a fresh-water habitat?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: a river. Rivers, streams and ponds are fresh-water habitats; the sea is a sea-water habitat and the estuary has brackish water.

mcqs.q: A grassland habitat is best described as:
options: Hot and dry with very little rain
mcqs.why: Correct answer: grassy plains. Forests have heavy rain and dense trees, deserts are hot and dry, and tundra is covered with snow — grasslands are wide plains of grass.

mcqs.q: Which things does an organism get from its habitat?
options: Food, shelter, protection and facilities to reproduce
mcqs.why: Correct answer: food, shelter, protection and facilities to reproduce. A habitat provides everything an organism needs to live and continue its kind.

mcqs.q: Whales and sharks are examples of animals that:
options: Live both on land and in water equally
mcqs.why: Correct answer: they live only in water. Water animals' bodies are made for the water environment — they obtain oxygen and food from the water and swim in it.

mcqs.q: Every habitat has its own special conditions of:
options: Temperature, light, moisture, soil and water
mcqs.why: Correct answer: temperature, light, moisture, soil and water. These conditions differ from habitat to habitat, and organisms are suited to the conditions of their own habitat.

mcqs.q: The estuarine habitat is found:
options: Where the river meets the sea
In the middle of a desert
mcqs.why: Correct answer: where the river meets the sea. Its water is brackish because fresh river water and salty sea water mix there.

lessons.title: Ecosystem, Population and Community
lessons.notes_html:
Three Important Terms

TermMeaning
EcosystemThe combined system of the living (biotic) part and the non-living (abiotic) part of a place, in which both interact with each other
PopulationA group of organisms of the same species living in a particular habitat
CommunityAll the different populations (plants, animals and micro-organisms) living together in one habitat

The interaction of organisms with one another and with the environment forms the ecosystem.

Daily Changes in a Habitat

  • The difference between day and night.
  • Light intensity and temperature change — more light and heat in the day, less at night.
  • Because of this, some animals are active in the day (diurnal) and some at night (nocturnal).

Yearly Changes in a Habitat

  • The coming of the four seasons.
  • Differences in temperature and rainfall through the year.
  • Natural disasters such as drought, flood and earthquake.
  • Human activity, such as global warming.

mcqs.q: The interaction of organisms with one another and with the environment is called an:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: ecosystem. When the living (biotic) and non-living (abiotic) parts of a place interact together, that combined system is the ecosystem.

mcqs.q: An ecosystem is made of:
options: The living part and the non-living part interacting together
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the living (biotic) part and the non-living (abiotic) part together, interacting with each other — for example, plants, animals, soil, water and sunlight in a pond.

mcqs.q: A population is:
options: All the different populations in one habitat
A series of organisms eating one another
A group of organisms of the same species living in a particular habitat
The non-living part of a place
mcqs.why: Correct answer: a population is a group of organisms of the SAME species in a particular habitat — for example, all the frogs in one pond.

mcqs.q: A community is:
options: Only the animals of a place
The soil and water of a place
All the different populations living together in one habitat
mcqs.why: Correct answer: a community is all the different populations — plants, animals and micro-organisms — living together in one habitat.

mcqs.q: Which factor causes daily changes in a habitat?
options: The difference between day and night, with changes in light and temperature
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the day–night difference. Light intensity and temperature are higher in the day and lower at night, so daily life in the habitat changes.

mcqs.q: Animals that are active at night are called:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: nocturnal. Animals active in the day are diurnal; those active at night are nocturnal — both are responses to the daily changes of light and temperature.

mcqs.q: Which of these causes yearly changes in a habitat?
options: The coming of the four seasons
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the four seasons. Seasons, yearly differences in temperature and rainfall, natural disasters and human activity change a habitat over the year.

mcqs.q: In the term 'ecosystem', the abiotic part means:
options: The non-living part, such as soil, water and sunlight
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the abiotic part is the non-living part of the place. The ecosystem is the biotic (living) part and the abiotic (non-living) part working together.

mcqs.q: All the frogs, fish, plants and microbes living together in one pond make up the pond's:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: community — because a community is all the DIFFERENT populations living together in one habitat. Only the frogs alone would be a population.

mcqs.q: Which is a human activity that changes habitats over the year?
options: Global warming caused by human activity
mcqs.why: Correct answer: global warming from human activity is listed among the causes of yearly (long-term) changes in habitats, along with seasons, rainfall differences and natural disasters.

lessons.title: Adaptation — How Living Things Fit Their Habitat
lessons.notes_html:
What Is Adaptation?

The conditions of every place are different — light, temperature, moisture, air, soil and water. Organisms survive by taking on special features suited to those conditions. This is called adaptation.

How Animals Adapt

  • Camouflage — changing colour or appearance to match the surroundings.
  • Migration — moving from one place to another when conditions change.
  • Hibernation — a long winter sleep.
  • Aestivation — a long summer sleep.
  • Body covering — for example, thick fur or a fatty covering in cold regions.

How Plants Adapt

  • Shedding leaves in hard seasons.
  • Changing their structure to suit the place.

Examples

  • The earthworm lives in burrows in the ground and is adapted to its environment.
  • The skin colour of people living in hot regions helps protect them from the heat of the sun.
  • In cold regions, animals have thick fur or a fatty covering to keep warm.
  • Water animals have bodies made for swimming and for obtaining oxygen and food from the water.

mcqs.q: Changing colour or appearance to match the surroundings is called:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: camouflage. It is one of the special characteristics by which organisms adapt to the changing conditions of the environment.

mcqs.q: A long winter sleep is called:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: hibernation. Animals sleep through the cold winter; the long SUMMER sleep is called aestivation.

mcqs.q: A long summer sleep is called:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: aestivation. It is the summer counterpart of hibernation — animals rest through the hot, dry season.

mcqs.q: Moving from one place to another when conditions change is called:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: migration. Birds and other animals migrate to places where food and weather are suitable — one of the ways organisms adapt to changing conditions.

mcqs.q: How do plants adapt to different conditions?
options: By shedding leaves and changing their structure
mcqs.why: Correct answer: plants adapt by shedding leaves and changing their structure to suit the light, temperature, moisture and soil of the place.

mcqs.q: Animals in cold regions are protected by:
options: Thick fur or a fatty covering
mcqs.why: Correct answer: thick fur or a fatty covering keeps cold-region animals warm — a body-covering adaptation to very cold habitats like the tundra.

mcqs.q: The earthworm is adapted to its environment because it:
options: Lives in burrows in the ground
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the earthworm lives in burrows in the ground and is adapted to life in the soil — its body and habits suit its habitat.

mcqs.q: The skin colour of people in hot regions helps them by:
options: Protecting them from the heat of the sun
mcqs.why: Correct answer: darker skin colour in hot regions helps protect people from the strong heat of the sun — an example of adaptation in human beings.

mcqs.q: Adaptation means:
options: Eating only one kind of food
Having special characteristics that suit an organism to its environment
mcqs.why: Correct answer: adaptation is the set of special characteristics — like camouflage, migration, hibernation, body covering and leaf-shedding — that help organisms live in their environment.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT an animal adaptation given in this chapter?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: shedding leaves is a PLANT adaptation. Camouflage, migration and hibernation (and aestivation and body covering) are animal adaptations.

lessons.title: Food Chains, Food Webs and Protecting Habitats
lessons.notes_html:
Food Chain

A food chain is a series of organisms in which each organism gets food and energy from the previous organism. A food chain always starts from the producers (plants), because plants prepare their own food with sunlight; the food then passes to the consumers.

  • Example 1: Grass → Grasshopper → Frog → Snake → Hawk
  • Example 2: Grass → Rat → Hawk

Food Web

A food web is a web made of many food chains joined together, because one organism can get food from several sources.

  • Example: Grass and plants → Grasshopper → Frog → Hawk, and grass and plants → Rat → Hawk.
  • Example: Grass and plants → Crow → Snake → Hawk, and grass and plants → Crow → Hawk.

People Change Habitats

People change their place of living and change habitats for their needs — for example, using land for settlements and farming. Human activities also create pollution and global warming, which change habitats.

Protecting a Habitat

  • Reduce pollution.
  • Save forests and natural areas from destruction.
  • Keep the balance of the environment.

mcqs.q: A food chain always starts from the:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the producers. The producers (plants) prepare their own food with sunlight, and then that food and energy pass on to the consumers.

mcqs.q: A food chain is:
options: A series of organisms in which each gets food and energy from the previous one
A group of the same species
The non-living part of a habitat
mcqs.why: Correct answer: a food chain is a single series — for example, Grass → Grasshopper → Frog → Snake → Hawk — in which each organism feeds on the previous one.

mcqs.q: A food web differs from a food chain because it is:
options: Made of many food chains joined together, since one organism can eat from several sources
mcqs.why: Correct answer: a food web joins many food chains together. In real life one organism (like a hawk) can get food from several sources, so the chains link into a web.

mcqs.q: In the chain Grass → Grasshopper → Frog → Snake → Hawk, the producer is:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: grass. The producer makes its own food with sunlight and starts the chain; all the others are consumers that depend on it directly or indirectly.

mcqs.q: Why do people change their place of living (habitat)?
options: For their needs — for example land for settlements and farming
mcqs.why: Correct answer: people change habitats for their needs, such as using land for settlements and farming. Their activities also create pollution and global warming, which further change habitats.

mcqs.q: To protect a habitat, we should:
options: Reduce pollution and save forests and natural areas
Destroy the balance of the environment
mcqs.why: Correct answer: pollution must be reduced, forests and natural areas must be saved from destruction, and the balance of the environment must be kept.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a correct food chain from the book?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: Grass → Rat → Hawk. Every food chain starts with a producer (grass), then a consumer that eats it (rat), then a consumer that eats that animal (hawk).

mcqs.q: Human activities change habitats by creating:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: human activities create pollution and global warming, which change the conditions of habitats and make life harder for the organisms living there.

mcqs.q: In a food web, one organism can:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: one organism can get food from several sources — that is exactly why many food chains join together to form a food web.

mcqs.q: Keeping the balance of the environment is important because:
options: It protects habitats and the organisms living in them
mcqs.why: Correct answer: a balanced environment protects habitats. Reducing pollution and saving forests and natural areas keeps the balance on which all living things depend.

lessons.title: The Water Cycle and Why Water Is Necessary
lessons.notes_html:
The Water Cycle

All the movement and circulation of water on the earth is called the water cycle. The water cycle keeps the environment balanced, and clean water is necessary for the pleasant, healthy working of the environment.

Why Water Is Necessary for Animals

  • Animals drink water every day.
  • Their food also contains water.
  • Without water animals cannot stay alive.
  • Plants need water to make food (photosynthesis), and plants are the source of food for animals.

So water is a basic need of life for animals, plants and human beings alike.

A Gift From the Sea

Sea weeds and sea plants are used to make fertilizer — one of the useful things water habitats give us.

Clean Water and the Environment

Clean water is necessary for the life of plants, animals and human beings, and the water cycle keeps the environment balanced. Dirty water spoils the environment and spreads diseases.

mcqs.q: All the movement and circulation of water on the earth is called the:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the water cycle. Water keeps moving and circulating on the earth, and this circulation keeps the environment balanced.

mcqs.q: Sea weeds and sea plants are used to make:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: fertilizer. Sea weeds and sea plants collected from the sea are used as fertilizer for crops.

mcqs.q: Which of these shows that water is necessary for animals?
options: Animals drink water every day and their food also contains water
Animals need water only in winter
Animals get water only from rain
mcqs.why: Correct answer: animals drink water daily, their food contains water, and without water they cannot stay alive — water is a basic need for animals.

mcqs.q: Plants need water mainly to:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: plants need water to make food (photosynthesis). Since plants are the source of food for animals, animals depend on water indirectly too.

mcqs.q: Why is clean water necessary for a pleasant environment?
options: It is necessary for the life of plants, animals and humans, and the water cycle keeps the environment balanced
mcqs.why: Correct answer: clean water supports the life of plants, animals and human beings, and the water cycle keeps the environment balanced. Dirty water spoils the environment and spreads diseases.

mcqs.q: Dirty water harms the environment because it:
options: Spoils the environment and spreads diseases
mcqs.why: Correct answer: dirty water spoils the environment and spreads diseases among plants, animals and people — that is why keeping water clean matters.

mcqs.q: Animals get water from:
options: Drinking and from the food they eat
mcqs.why: Correct answer: animals drink water every day, and their food also contains water. Both sources together meet the body's need.

mcqs.q: The water cycle is important because it:
options: Keeps the environment balanced by moving water around the earth
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the water cycle keeps the environment balanced — water circulates between the earth, water bodies and the air, supporting all life.

mcqs.q: Which statement is TRUE?
options: Animals can stay alive without water
Plants are a source of food for animals and need water for photosynthesis
mcqs.why: Correct answer: plants need water for photosynthesis and are the food source of animals, so water is necessary for animals both directly (drinking) and indirectly (food).

mcqs.q: Water is called a basic need of life because:
options: It is used only for washing
No plant, animal or human can live without it
It is found only in rivers
mcqs.why: Correct answer: water is a basic need for life — animals drink it daily, plants need it to make food, and without it living things cannot stay alive.

lessons.title: Making Water Safe to Drink
lessons.notes_html:
Boiling Makes Water Safe

To make water fit for drinking, it is boiled for 15 to 20 minutes. Boiling kills the disease-causing germs in the water, so boiled water becomes safe and suitable for drinking and cooking.

Why Unclean Water Causes Diseases

If water does not meet the standard of clean water, it contains:

  • Disease-causing germs (bacteria and viruses).
  • Chemical substances.
  • Particles of pesticides.

Such water causes diseases like hepatitis, cholera, typhoid and diarrhoea.

What Is Found in Water (from the project)

KindExamples
Physical thingsSand, clay, suspended particles
Chemical thingsSalts, pesticides (such as DDT), factory chemicals
Biological thingsBacteria, viruses and other disease-causing germs

Desalination — Removing Salt

Removing salt from saline (salty) water is called desalination. Salt is separated so that the water can be used for drinking, domestic work and recreation.

mcqs.q: To make water fit for drinking, it should be boiled for:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: 15 to 20 minutes. Boiling for this time kills the disease-causing germs, making the water safe for drinking and cooking.

mcqs.q: Why is boiled water suitable for drinking and cooking?
options: Boiling kills the disease-causing germs in it
mcqs.why: Correct answer: boiling water for 15–20 minutes kills the germs that cause diseases, so boiled water becomes safe for drinking and cooking.

mcqs.q: Unclean water can cause which diseases?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: hepatitis, cholera, typhoid, diarrhoea and other diseases. Such water contains disease-causing germs, chemical substances and pesticide particles.

mcqs.q: Which of these are the biological things found in water?
options: Bacteria, viruses and other disease-causing germs
mcqs.why: Correct answer: bacteria, viruses and other germs are the biological things in water. Sand and clay are physical things; salts and pesticides like DDT are chemical things.

mcqs.q: DDT in water is an example of a:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: DDT is a chemical thing — a pesticide. Chemical things in water include salts, pesticides and factory chemicals.

mcqs.q: Removing salt from saline water is called:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: desalination. Salt is separated from saline water so it can be used for drinking, domestic work and recreation.

mcqs.q: Desalinated water is used for:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: after desalination, the water is used for drinking, domestic work and recreation — it becomes ordinary usable water.

mcqs.q: Sand and clay in water are examples of:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: physical things — sand, clay and suspended particles. They make water muddy and are removed by settling and filtration in cleaning plants.

mcqs.q: Water that does not meet the clean-water standard is dangerous because it contains:
options: Germs, chemical substances and pesticide particles
mcqs.why: Correct answer: it contains disease-causing germs, chemical substances and particles of pesticides, which cause diseases like cholera, typhoid and hepatitis.

mcqs.q: The simplest home method to make water safe is:
options: Keeping it in sunlight for a day
mcqs.why: Correct answer: boiling for 15 to 20 minutes. It kills the germs without any chemicals, so the water becomes fit for drinking and cooking.

lessons.title: Cleaning Water in Treatment Plants
lessons.notes_html:
Matching the Cleaning Helpers

HelperIts work
Potash alum (a flocculant)Makes the tiny things in water stick together into large particles/flocculates, which settle down
Liquid chlorineDestroys harmful microbes (germs)
DistillationSeparates water from dirt and physical and chemical things: water is boiled into vapour and then cooled to get clean water

How a Water Treatment Plant Works

  • Step 1 — Flocculation: a flocculant chemical is mixed into the water to gather the tiny particles of sand and pesticides into large clumps (flocculates), which settle at the bottom.
  • Step 2 — Filtration: the water is filtered through sand and stones.
  • Step 3 — Chlorination: chlorine is mixed in to kill disease-causing germs.
  • Step 4 — Supply: the clean water is sent to homes and factories.

RO Filter Plant

In an RO (Reverse Osmosis) filter plant, water is passed through a semi-permeable membrane, which stops salts, chemical substances and germs, letting clean water pass.

Model Plant (Project)

The book's project model shows the same parts in order: a dirty-water tank → flocculation section → filter (sand and stones) section → chlorination section → clean-water tank, each part labelled.

mcqs.q: In water-cleaning plants, a ______ is used to gather together the tiny particles of sand and pesticides.
mcqs.why: Correct answer: a flocculant chemical. It makes the tiny particles gather into large clumps called flocculates, which settle at the bottom of the tank.

mcqs.q: Potash alum cleans water by:
options: Making the things in water stick together into large particles
mcqs.why: Correct answer: potash alum is a flocculant — it makes the tiny things present in the water stick together into large particles that settle down.

mcqs.q: Liquid chlorine is used in water cleaning to:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: liquid chlorine destroys harmful microbes (germs). It is mixed into the water in the chlorination step, after filtration.

mcqs.q: Distillation separates water from dirt by:
options: Boiling water into vapour and then cooling it to obtain clean water
mcqs.why: Correct answer: in distillation the water is boiled into vapour and then cooled, giving clean water separated from dirt and physical and chemical things.

mcqs.q: The correct order of steps in a water treatment plant is:
options: Flocculation → filtration through sand and stones → chlorination → supply
mcqs.why: Correct answer: first flocculation settles the particles, then filtration through sand and stones, then chlorination kills germs, and finally the clean water is sent to homes and factories.

mcqs.q: In an RO filter plant, water passes through a:
options: Semi-permeable membrane that stops salts, chemicals and germs
mcqs.why: Correct answer: a semi-permeable membrane. In Reverse Osmosis the membrane stops salts, chemical substances and germs, and clean water passes through.

mcqs.q: The large clumps formed by a flocculant are called:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: flocculates. The flocculant chemical gathers tiny particles of sand and pesticides into these large clumps, which settle at the bottom.

mcqs.q: After chlorination, the clean water in a treatment plant is:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the clean water is sent to homes and factories for use. Chlorination is the last cleaning step before supply.

mcqs.q: In the model water-cleaning plant project, the filter section contains:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the filter section holds sand and stones, through which the water passes after flocculation and becomes physically clean.

mcqs.q: Filtration in a treatment plant removes:
options: Sand, stones and settled particles from the water
mcqs.why: Correct answer: filtration through sand and stones removes the physical particles. Germs are killed later by chlorination, not by the filter.

lessons.title: Saving Water — Stopping Wastage
lessons.notes_html:
Why Are Pakistan's Fresh-Water Reserves Running Out?

  • Fresh water is not preserved and protected for domestic, agricultural and industrial use.
  • Water is being polluted by domestic, industrial and agricultural waste.
  • Wastage of water and increasing use are also reducing the reserves.

Five Ways to Reduce Wastage of Water in Daily Life

  • Get leaking taps and pipes repaired at once.
  • Do not leave the tap running while brushing your teeth or washing your hands and face.
  • Use water carefully while bathing, and turn off the shower while applying soap.
  • Use a bucket instead of a hose pipe to wash a car.
  • Run the washing machine only when it has a full load, and water the garden in the morning or evening so the moisture stays in the soil for a long time.

mcqs.q: Pakistan's fresh-water reserves are running out mainly because:
options: Fresh water is not preserved or protected, and it is polluted by domestic, industrial and agricultural waste
There is no rain at all
mcqs.why: Correct answer: fresh water is not preserved and protected for domestic, agricultural and industrial use, and waste from homes, industries and farms pollutes it. Wastage and increasing use add to the problem.

mcqs.q: Which waste pollutes Pakistan's fresh water?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: domestic (home), industrial (factory) and agricultural (farm) waste all pollute the fresh water and reduce the usable reserves.

mcqs.q: The first step to stop water wastage at home is to:
options: Get leaking taps and pipes repaired at once
mcqs.why: Correct answer: repair leaking taps and pipes at once. A leaking tap wastes water drop by drop all day and night.

mcqs.q: While brushing your teeth, you should:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: do not leave the tap running while brushing your teeth or washing your hands and face — turn it on only when you need the water.

mcqs.q: To wash a car with less water, use:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: use a bucket instead of a hose pipe. A hose pipe keeps water flowing and wastes far more than a bucket.

mcqs.q: The washing machine should be run:
options: Only when it has a full load
mcqs.why: Correct answer: run the washing machine only when it has a full load, so the same water washes more clothes and less water is wasted.

mcqs.q: The garden should be watered in the morning or evening so that:
options: The moisture stays in the soil for a long time
mcqs.why: Correct answer: in the morning or evening less water evaporates in the heat, so the moisture stays in the soil for a long time and plants get more benefit.

mcqs.q: While applying soap during a bath, you should:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: turn off the shower while applying soap. Using water carefully while bathing is one of the book's five ways to reduce wastage.

mcqs.q: Increasing use and wastage of water both:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: wastage and ever-increasing use are reducing Pakistan's fresh-water reserves, together with pollution and poor protection of water.

mcqs.q: Saving water is important because:
options: Fresh-water reserves are limited and are running out
mcqs.why: Correct answer: fresh-water reserves are limited and running out due to pollution, wastage and increasing use — so every person should reduce wastage in daily life.

lessons.title: Inside the Atom — Nucleus, Protons, Neutrons and Electrons
lessons.notes_html:
Inside the Atom

ParticleChargeWhere it is
ProtonPositive (+)In the nucleus
NeutronNo chargeIn the nucleus
ElectronNegative (−)Revolving around the nucleus in shells

The Nucleus Has a Positive Charge

The centre of the atom — the nucleus — has a positive charge, because it contains positively charged protons and neutrons which have no charge.

Where Is the Mass of the Atom?

Almost the whole mass of an atom is in the nucleus, because the protons and neutrons are there and the mass of an electron is very small. The mass number of an atom = number of protons + number of neutrons.

A Neutral Atom

An atom in which the number of protons is equal to the number of electrons has no overall charge. Such an atom is called a neutral atom.

mcqs.q: What kind of charge is there on the nucleus of an atom?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: positive. The nucleus contains positively charged protons and neutrons with no charge, so the nucleus as a whole is positively charged.

mcqs.q: Which particles keep revolving around the nucleus?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: electrons. They revolve around the nucleus in different orbits or shells, which are named K, L, M and so on.

mcqs.q: A neutral atom is an atom in which:
options: The number of protons is equal to the number of electrons, so it has no overall charge
mcqs.why: Correct answer: a neutral atom has equal numbers of protons (+) and electrons (−), so the charges cancel and the atom has no overall charge.

mcqs.q: The whole mass of an atom is contained in:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: in the nucleus. Almost the whole mass of an atom is in the nucleus because protons and neutrons are there; an electron's mass is very small.

mcqs.q: The mass of an atom is equal to the mass of its:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: neutrons and protons. Mass number = number of protons + number of neutrons; electrons are so light that their mass is not counted.

mcqs.q: An atom has 11 protons and 12 neutrons. Its mass number is:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: 23. Mass number = protons + neutrons = 11 + 12 = 23. (This is sodium: atomic number 11, mass number 23.)

mcqs.q: Neutrons are particles that have:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: neutrons have no charge. They sit in the nucleus with the positively charged protons and add to the atom's mass.

mcqs.q: Electrons revolve around the nucleus in:
options: Orbits or shells named K, L, M…
mcqs.why: Correct answer: electrons revolve in orbits or shells around the nucleus. The first shell is K, then L, then M, then N.

mcqs.q: If an atom has 8 protons, how many electrons does a neutral atom of it have?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: 8. In a neutral atom the number of electrons equals the number of protons, so the positive and negative charges balance.

mcqs.q: The atomic number of an atom is equal to its number of:
options: Electrons in the outer shell only
mcqs.why: Correct answer: protons. An atom with atomic number 16 has 16 protons — the atomic number is the identity of the element.

lessons.title: Electron Arrangement in Shells
lessons.notes_html:
How Electrons Are Arranged in Shells

Electrons fill the shells K, L, M, N in order. From the book's structure diagrams:

Element (atomic number)KLMN
Magnesium (12)282—
Aluminium (13)283—
Silicon (14)284—
Sulphur (16)286—
Chlorine (17)287—
Calcium (20)2882
Sodium (11)281—

Valence Electrons

The electrons in the outermost shell are called valence electrons:

  • Nitrogen (2, 5) → 5 valence electrons.
  • Helium (2) → 2 valence electrons; its only shell is complete.
  • Lithium (2, 1) → 1 valence electron.

Elements such as hydrogen, lithium, sodium and potassium have only one electron in their outermost shell, so their valency is 1.

Making Atom Models (Project)

Models of atoms are made with a nucleus in the centre (balls of different colours for protons and neutrons) and wire orbits (shells) around it with balls for the electrons — for example, calcium 2, 8, 8, 2 and chlorine 2, 8, 7.

mcqs.q: The electron arrangement of magnesium (atomic number 12) is:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: 2, 8, 2. Magnesium has 12 electrons: 2 in the K shell, 8 in the L shell and 2 in the M shell.

mcqs.q: How many electrons are in the valence shell of nitrogen (arrangement 2, 5)?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: 5. The valence shell is the outermost shell; nitrogen's arrangement is 2, 5, so its M shell (outermost) holds 5 electrons.

mcqs.q: Helium has 2 valence electrons because:
options: Its only shell (K) contains 2 electrons and is complete
mcqs.why: Correct answer: helium's arrangement is just (2) — its only shell is the K shell with 2 electrons, and that shell is complete, so both electrons are valence electrons.

mcqs.q: Lithium (2, 1) has how many valence electrons?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: 1. Lithium's outermost (L) shell holds a single electron, so its valency is 1 — like hydrogen, sodium and potassium.

mcqs.q: Which elements have only one electron in their outermost shell?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: hydrogen, lithium, sodium and potassium each have only one electron in their outermost shell, so their valency is 1.

mcqs.q: The electron arrangement of calcium (20) is:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: 2, 8, 8, 2. Calcium's 20 electrons fill K with 2, L with 8, M with 8, and the remaining 2 go into the N shell.

mcqs.q: Sulphur (16) has how many electrons in its outermost shell?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: 6. Sulphur's arrangement is 2, 8, 6, so the outermost (M) shell contains 6 valence electrons.

mcqs.q: In the atom model project, the shells are shown by:
options: Wire orbits around the nucleus with balls for electrons
mcqs.why: Correct answer: wire orbits (shells) are placed around a central nucleus of coloured balls (protons and neutrons), with balls on the wires for the electrons — for example calcium 2, 8, 8, 2.

mcqs.q: The outermost shell of an atom is important because its electrons are the:
options: Valence electrons, which decide the valency
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the outermost shell's electrons are the valence electrons. Lithium, sodium and potassium have 1 valence electron each, so their valency is 1.

mcqs.q: Silicon (14) has the arrangement:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: 2, 8, 4. Silicon's 14 electrons are arranged 2 in K, 8 in L and 4 in M, giving it 4 valence electrons.

lessons.title: Ions — Cations and Anions
lessons.notes_html:
Cations and Anions

CationAnion
Formed when an atom gives away an electronFormed when an atom gains an electron
Becomes positively charged (+)Becomes negatively charged (−)
Example: Na⁺ (sodium)Example: Cl⁻ (chlorine)

Why? Losing a negative electron leaves more protons than electrons, so the ion is positive. Gaining an electron gives more electrons than protons, so the ion is negative.

Ions of Some Elements (from the book's chart)

ElementIonProtonsElectrons in the ion
AluminiumAl³⁺1310
ChlorineCl⁻1718
SodiumNa⁺1110
PotassiumK⁺1918

Note: the number of protons never changes when an ion forms — only electrons are lost or gained.

mcqs.q: A cation is formed when an atom:
options: Gives away an electron and becomes positively charged
mcqs.why: Correct answer: a cation forms when an atom gives away an electron. With one negative charge gone, protons outnumber electrons and the ion is positive — for example Na⁺.

mcqs.q: An anion is formed when an atom:
options: Gains an electron and becomes negatively charged
mcqs.why: Correct answer: an anion forms when an atom gains an electron, so electrons outnumber protons and the ion is negative — for example Cl⁻.

mcqs.q: The sodium ion Na⁺ has:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: 11 protons and 10 electrons. The sodium atom lost one electron, so only the electron count changed; the protons stay 11.

mcqs.q: The chloride ion Cl⁻ has 17 protons and:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: 18 electrons. Chlorine gained one electron (17 + 1 = 18), which is why the ion carries a single negative charge.

mcqs.q: The aluminium ion is Al³⁺ because the aluminium atom:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: aluminium loses its 3 valence electrons, leaving 13 protons and 10 electrons — a charge of 3+ (Al³⁺).

mcqs.q: When an ion forms, which number never changes?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the number of protons never changes. Only electrons are lost or gained; that is why Na still has 11 protons as Na⁺ and Cl still has 17 as Cl⁻.

mcqs.q: Potassium forms the ion K⁺ with 19 protons and how many electrons?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: 18 electrons. Potassium loses its one outer electron (19 − 1 = 18), giving the K⁺ ion a single positive charge.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an anion?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: Cl⁻ is an anion — a negatively charged ion. Na⁺, K⁺ and Al³⁺ are cations, which are positively charged.

mcqs.q: An atom that gains two electrons will carry a charge of:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: 2−. Each gained electron adds one negative charge, so two gained electrons make the ion twice negatively charged — an anion.

mcqs.q: Why does a cation have a positive charge?
options: After losing electrons it has more protons than electrons
mcqs.why: Correct answer: a cation has more protons (+) than electrons (−) because the atom gave away electrons. The unbalanced positive charge is what makes it positive.

lessons.title: Atomic Number, Mass Number and Isotopes
lessons.notes_html:
Atomic Number and Mass Number

  • Atomic number = number of protons. An atom with atomic number 16 has 16 protons.
  • Mass number = protons + neutrons.
  • Number of neutrons = mass number − atomic number.

Isotopes

Atoms of the same element which have different mass numbers are called isotopes. They have the same atomic number (same protons) but different numbers of neutrons.

Reading the Book's Chart

ElementAtomic no.Mass no.ProtonsNeutronsElectronsIsotope name
Carbon (C)612666Carbon-12
Magnesium (Mg)1224121212Magnesium-24
Chlorine (Cl)1735171817Chlorine-35
Aluminium (Al)1327131413Aluminium-27

mcqs.q: Atoms of the same element which have different mass numbers are called:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: isotopes. They have the same atomic number but different mass numbers, because their numbers of neutrons differ.

mcqs.q: An atom has atomic number 16 and mass number 32. How many protons does it have?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: 16. The number of protons is equal to the atomic number — always. (Its neutrons are 32 − 16 = 16.)

mcqs.q: For the same atom (atomic number 16, mass number 32), the number of neutrons is:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: 16. Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 32 − 16 = 16.

mcqs.q: Chlorine-35 has atomic number 17. Its number of neutrons is:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: 18. Neutrons = 35 − 17 = 18, while its protons and (in the neutral atom) electrons are both 17.

mcqs.q: Isotopes of an element have the same:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: atomic number. Isotopes are the same element, so their protons (atomic number) are the same; only the neutrons — and therefore the mass number — differ.

mcqs.q: Carbon-12 has 6 protons. Its number of neutrons is:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: 6. Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 12 − 6 = 6. Carbon-12 has 6 protons, 6 neutrons and 6 electrons.

mcqs.q: Magnesium-24 (atomic number 12) has:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: 12 neutrons (24 − 12 = 12). It also has 12 protons and 12 electrons, as shown in the book's chart.

mcqs.q: Aluminium-27 (atomic number 13) has how many neutrons?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: 14 neutrons (27 − 13 = 14). Aluminium-27 has 13 protons, 14 neutrons and 13 electrons.

mcqs.q: The mass number of an atom is:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: mass number = number of protons + number of neutrons. Electrons are not counted because their mass is very small.

mcqs.q: Two atoms with the same atomic number but mass numbers 35 and 37 are:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: they are isotopes of the same element — same protons (same atomic number), different neutrons, so different mass numbers.

lessons.title: Chemical Formulas and Molecules
lessons.notes_html:
What a Chemical Formula Shows

A chemical formula shows the number of atoms of each element in a compound. For example, H₂O tells us that one molecule of water contains 2 atoms of hydrogen and 1 atom of oxygen.

Counting Atoms in Formulas

CompoundElementsRatio of atoms
Water — H₂OHydrogen, oxygenH : O = 2 : 1
Aluminium oxide — Al₂O₃Aluminium, oxygenAl : O = 2 : 3
Calcium oxide — CaOCalcium, oxygenCa : O = 1 : 1
Hydrochloric acid — HClHydrogen, chlorineH : Cl = 1 : 1
Calcium fluoride — CaF₂Calcium, fluorineCa : F = 1 : 2

Two Molecules to Remember

  • Methane (CH₄) — 1 atom of carbon and 4 atoms of hydrogen.
  • Ammonia (NH₃) — 1 atom of nitrogen and 3 atoms of hydrogen.

The small number written below and after a symbol (subscript) tells how many atoms of that element are present. If there is no number, it means one atom.

mcqs.q: What does a chemical formula show?
options: The number of atoms in a molecule only
The number of atoms of each element in the compound
mcqs.why: Correct answer: a chemical formula shows the number of atoms of each element — for example, H₂O shows 2 atoms of hydrogen and 1 atom of oxygen in one water molecule.

mcqs.q: How many carbon and hydrogen atoms are there in methane (CH₄)?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: methane has 1 atom of carbon and 4 atoms of hydrogen. The subscript 4 after H shows the four hydrogen atoms; C has no subscript, so it is one atom.

mcqs.q: The chemical formula of ammonia is:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: NH₃. One molecule of ammonia contains 1 atom of nitrogen and 3 atoms of hydrogen.

mcqs.q: In aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃), the ratio of aluminium to oxygen atoms is:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: Al : O = 2 : 3. The subscripts in Al₂O₃ show 2 atoms of aluminium joined with 3 atoms of oxygen.

mcqs.q: In calcium fluoride (CaF₂), the ratio Ca : F is:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: Ca : F = 1 : 2. There is 1 atom of calcium (no subscript) and 2 atoms of fluorine in CaF₂.

mcqs.q: The formula HCl shows that hydrochloric acid contains:
options: 1 atom of hydrogen and 1 atom of chlorine
mcqs.why: Correct answer: 1 atom of hydrogen and 1 atom of chlorine — a ratio of 1 : 1, because neither symbol carries a subscript.

mcqs.q: In water (H₂O), the ratio of hydrogen to oxygen atoms is:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: H : O = 2 : 1. Two atoms of hydrogen combine with one atom of oxygen in each water molecule.

mcqs.q: CaO (calcium oxide) contains calcium and oxygen in the ratio:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: Ca : O = 1 : 1. Neither symbol in CaO has a subscript, so there is one atom of each element.

mcqs.q: If a formula shows no number after an element's symbol, it means there is:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: one atom. For example, the C in CH₄ and the Ca in CaF₂ each stand for a single atom of that element.

mcqs.q: How many atoms in total are there in one molecule of ammonia (NH₃)?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: 4 atoms — 1 nitrogen + 3 hydrogen = 4 atoms in each ammonia molecule.

lessons.title: Physical and Chemical Changes — The Difference
lessons.notes_html:
Physical Change and Chemical Change

Physical changeChemical change
Only the shape, state, size or texture changes; the chemical composition does NOT changeThe chemical composition changes and a new thing is produced, with completely different properties
Usually reversible (temporary)Usually irreversible
Examples: ice turning into water, tearing paper into piecesExamples: paper burning, iron rusting, photosynthesis

Quick Tests From the Book

  • Melting of ice cream → physical change (only the state changes).
  • An irreversible change is called a chemical change.
  • Burning of a candle → chemical change (wax burns and makes carbon dioxide and water vapour).
  • Obtaining salt from sea water → physical change (water evaporates, salt is obtained in its original state).
  • A temporary change is called a physical change.
  • Water turning into ice, mixing things together, and separating a mixture are all physical changes — mixing makes no new thing, and separating gives each thing back in its original state.

Sorting Changes (from the book's exercise)

Reversible (physical)Irreversible (chemical)
Twisting rubber; glass melting; ice turning into water; mixture of salt and sand; an electric bulb lighting up; dissolving sugar in waterA candle burning; photosynthesis; formation of glucose; formation of water by hydrogen and oxygen joining; paper burning into ash; boiling an egg

mcqs.q: In a physical change:
options: Only the shape, state, size or texture changes; the composition does not change
The change can never be reversed
mcqs.why: Correct answer: only the shape, state, size or texture of the matter changes, but its chemical composition does not change — for example, ice turning into water. Such changes are usually reversible.

mcqs.q: In a chemical change:
options: The composition changes and a new thing with completely different properties is produced
mcqs.why: Correct answer: a chemical change produces a new thing whose properties are completely different from the original — for example, paper burning or iron rusting. It is usually irreversible.
