mcqs.q: The melting of ice cream is a ______ type of change.
mcqs.why: Correct answer: physical. Only the state of the ice cream changes (solid to liquid); its composition stays the same, and it can be frozen again.

mcqs.q: An irreversible change is called a ______ type of change.
mcqs.why: Correct answer: chemical. Chemical changes are usually irreversible — the new substance formed cannot easily be changed back, like ash back into paper.

mcqs.q: The burning of a candle is a chemical change because:
options: The wax burns and makes new things — carbon dioxide and water vapour
mcqs.why: Correct answer: burning wax produces new substances (carbon dioxide and water vapour), so its composition changes — the sign of a chemical change.

mcqs.q: Obtaining salt from sea water is a physical change because:
options: The water evaporates and the salt is obtained in its original state
mcqs.why: Correct answer: it is physical — evaporation removes the water and the salt is recovered exactly as it was; no new substance is formed.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a reversible change?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: dissolving sugar in water is reversible (physical) — the sugar can be recovered by evaporation. Burning paper, boiling an egg and photosynthesis are irreversible chemical changes.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an irreversible change?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: formation of glucose is a chemical (irreversible) change. Twisting rubber, melting glass and a bulb lighting up are all reversible physical changes.

mcqs.q: Mixing things together and keeping them is a physical change because:
options: Mixing does not make any new thing
mcqs.why: Correct answer: mixing is physical — no new substance is formed, and separating the mixture gives each thing back in its original state.

mcqs.q: A temporary change is called a:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: physical change. Physical changes are temporary and can be reversed — for example, ice melts into water and the water can be frozen back into ice.

lessons.title: Changes Around Us at Home and School
lessons.notes_html:
Changes Happening Around Us

Physical changes at home, school and localityChemical changes at home, school and locality
Ice melting; water boiling and turning into vapour; tearing paper into pieces; salt dissolving in waterFood cooking; a candle burning; iron rusting; milk going sour

What Burning Produces

When something burns, apart from heat, light and water vapours, carbon dioxide gas is also produced.

Wood Rotting or Burning

When wood rots or burns, a chemical change takes place — wood burns to make ash and gases, which cannot turn back into wood.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a physical change at home?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: ice melting is physical — only the state changes. Food cooking, milk going sour and a candle burning are chemical changes from the book's list.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a chemical change at home?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: iron rusting is chemical — a new substance (rust) forms. Tearing paper, boiling water and dissolving salt are physical changes.

mcqs.q: When something burns, apart from heat, light and water vapours, what else is produced?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: carbon dioxide gas is produced when something burns, along with heat, light and water vapours.

mcqs.q: What change takes place when wood rots or burns?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: chemical change. Wood burns to make ash and gases, which cannot turn back into wood — a new substance has formed.

mcqs.q: Milk going sour is a:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: milk going sour is a chemical change — the milk changes into a new substance with new properties and cannot be turned back into fresh milk.

mcqs.q: Water boiling and turning into vapour is:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: it is a physical change. The water only changes state (liquid to vapour) and can be condensed back; its composition stays H₂O.

mcqs.q: Food cooking is listed in the book as a:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: cooking food is a chemical change — heat changes the substances in the food into new ones that cannot be changed back.

mcqs.q: Tearing paper into pieces is a physical change because:
options: Only the size and shape change; the paper is still paper
mcqs.why: Correct answer: only the size and shape change; the pieces are still paper, so its composition does not change.

mcqs.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: rusting of iron is a chemical change. Candle burning is also chemical (not physical), while dissolving salt and melting ice are physical.

mcqs.q: Salt dissolving in water can be reversed by:
options: Evaporating the water to get the salt back
mcqs.why: Correct answer: evaporating the water gives the salt back in its original state — which is why dissolving is a reversible, physical change.

lessons.title: Fuels — Why Hydrocarbons Are Burned
lessons.notes_html:
Hydrocarbons as Fuels

Hydrocarbons are used as fuel because they give heat and light when they burn.

Common Hydrocarbon Fuels

  • Natural gas (methane)
  • Petrol
  • Diesel
  • Furnace oil

These fuels are used in homes, factories and vehicles. Burning a fuel is a chemical change: the fuel burns and produces heat, light, water vapours and carbon dioxide gas.

mcqs.q: Why are hydrocarbons used as fuel?
options: They give heat and light when they burn
They cool the air when burned
mcqs.why: Correct answer: hydrocarbons give heat and light when they burn, which is exactly what a fuel must do. Natural gas, petrol, diesel and furnace oil are used in homes, factories and vehicles.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a hydrocarbon fuel?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: natural gas (methane) is a hydrocarbon fuel. Petrol, diesel and furnace oil are the other examples given in the book.

mcqs.q: Hydrocarbon fuels are used in:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: homes, factories and vehicles all burn hydrocarbon fuels — gas in homes, furnace oil in factories, and petrol and diesel in vehicles.

mcqs.q: Burning a fuel is an example of a:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: burning is a chemical change — the fuel changes into new substances (carbon dioxide and water vapour) and gives out heat and light.

mcqs.q: When a hydrocarbon fuel burns completely, the gas produced (besides water vapour) is:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: carbon dioxide. When something burns, apart from heat, light and water vapours, carbon dioxide gas is produced.

mcqs.q: Methane is the main part of:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: natural gas is mainly methane. It is one of the hydrocarbon fuels listed in the book.

mcqs.q: A good fuel must, when it burns, give out:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: heat and light. That is the very reason hydrocarbons are chosen as fuels for homes, factories and vehicles.

mcqs.q: Furnace oil is used as a fuel in:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: furnace oil is burned in factories. Together with natural gas, petrol and diesel, it is one of the book's hydrocarbon fuels.

mcqs.q: Petrol and diesel are mainly used in:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: vehicles run on petrol and diesel — two of the hydrocarbon fuels named in this chapter.

mcqs.q: Which statement is TRUE about fuels?
options: Fuels give heat and light when they burn
mcqs.why: Correct answer: fuels such as hydrocarbons give heat and light when they burn — a chemical change that also produces carbon dioxide and water vapour.

lessons.title: Fertilizers — Feeding the Soil
lessons.notes_html:
What Are Fertilizers?

Fertilizers are things that give nutrients to the soil so that the crop grows well. They fulfil the deficiency of nutrients in the soil — needs of plants that the soil alone cannot meet.

Properties of Fertilizers

Physical propertiesChemical properties (nutrients present)
Particle size, density, granule hardness, moisture contentNitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium, sulphur, carbon, hydrogen and oxygen

Why Fertilizers Must Not Be Used Improperly

  • Careless or excess use harms the environment.
  • It destroys the humus and fertility of the soil.
  • Nitrate enters crops and fruits and harms people.
  • So fertilizers should be used only on the advice of an agriculture expert.

mcqs.q: What are fertilizers?
options: Things that give nutrients to the soil so the crop grows well
mcqs.why: Correct answer: fertilizers give nutrients to the soil so crops grow well. They fulfil the deficiency of nutrients that plants need.

mcqs.q: What needs of plants are fulfilled by the use of fertilizer?
options: The deficiency of nutrients is fulfilled
mcqs.why: Correct answer: fertilizer fulfils the deficiency of nutrients — it gives the soil nutrients such as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium that crops need.

mcqs.q: Which of these are the nutrients present in fertilizers?
options: Nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium and sulphur
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the chemical properties of fertilizers are the nutrients in them — nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium, sulphur, carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.

mcqs.q: The physical properties of fertilizers include:
options: Particle size, density, granule hardness and moisture content
mcqs.why: Correct answer: particle size, density, granule hardness and moisture content are the physical properties; the nutrients present are the chemical properties.

mcqs.q: Why should fertilizers not be used in an improper way?
options: Excess use harms the environment, destroys soil humus and fertility, and nitrate enters crops and harms people
They make crops grow too fast only
mcqs.why: Correct answer: careless or excess use harms the environment, destroys the humus and fertility of the soil, and nitrate enters crops and fruits and harms people.

mcqs.q: Fertilizers should be used on the advice of:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: an agriculture expert. Expert advice ensures the right amount is used, so the soil and people are not harmed.

mcqs.q: Excess fertilizer destroys the ______ of the soil.
mcqs.why: Correct answer: excess fertilizer destroys the humus and fertility of the soil, so crops may actually suffer instead of growing well.

mcqs.q: Which harmful substance from fertilizers can enter crops and fruits?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: nitrate. When fertilizers are overused, nitrate enters crops and fruits and harms the people who eat them.

mcqs.q: Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium in a fertilizer are its:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: they are the chemical properties of the fertilizer — the nutrients it supplies to the soil and the crop.

mcqs.q: Using the right amount of fertilizer helps crops because:
options: It gives the soil the nutrients the crop needs to grow well
mcqs.why: Correct answer: fertilizer supplies missing nutrients to the soil so the crop grows well — that is its proper use, in the right amount and on expert advice.

lessons.title: Useful Chemical Changes — Ghee, Plastic and Projects
lessons.notes_html:
How Vegetable Oil Turns Into Ghee

Vegetable oil is changed into ghee (saturated fat/margarine) by the process of hydrogenation: hydrogen is mixed into vegetable oil in the presence of a nickel catalyst, which turns the unsaturated oil into saturated fat.

A Simple Method of Making Plastic

  • Mix borax powder in water in one cup.
  • In another cup, mix water and half a cup of white glue.
  • Slowly mix the glue mixture into the borax water, add drops of colour and mix well.
  • A soft, slimy substance (slime) forms — a simple plastic/polymer.

Two Project Observations

  • Plastic bottle sea: oil poured on blue water in a bottle does not mix with the water; it keeps floating on top in a separate layer — like oil pollution in the sea, which is harmful for sea life.
  • Dance of colours: when a cotton bud dipped in soapy water touches milk with colour drops, the colours dance and spread. The soap breaks the surface tension of the milk (a physical process) and reacts with the fat in the milk (a chemical process), pushing the colours around — a combination of physical and chemical changes.

mcqs.q: Which process is used to change vegetable oil into ghee?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: hydrogenation. Hydrogen is mixed into vegetable oil in the presence of a nickel catalyst, turning the unsaturated oil into saturated fat (ghee/margarine).

mcqs.q: In hydrogenation, the catalyst used is:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: nickel. Hydrogen is passed into the oil in the presence of a nickel catalyst to change the oil into ghee.

mcqs.q: Hydrogenation turns unsaturated oil into:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: saturated fat — ghee or margarine. The added hydrogen makes the oil thick and solid like ghee.

mcqs.q: In the simple plastic-making method, the slime is formed by mixing:
options: Borax water with a glue-and-water mixture
mcqs.why: Correct answer: borax solution is mixed slowly into the glue-and-water mixture; a soft, slimy substance forms, which is a simple plastic (polymer).

mcqs.q: In the plastic-bottle sea project, the oil on the water:
options: Does not mix and keeps floating on top in a separate layer
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the oil does not mix with the water; it floats on top as a separate layer. This shows the situation of oil pollution in the sea, which is harmful for sea life.

mcqs.q: Oil pollution in the sea is dangerous because it:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: oil floating on the sea is harmful for sea life — the project with the bottle, water, cooking oil and blue colour shows how the oil layer stays on the water.

mcqs.q: In the dance-of-colours project, the colours start dancing when:
options: A cotton bud dipped in soapy water touches the milk's surface
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the soapy bud touching the surface starts the dance — the soap breaks the surface tension and reacts with the fat in the milk, pushing the colours around.

mcqs.q: The work of the soap in the dance-of-colours activity is to:
options: Break the surface tension of the milk and react with its fat
mcqs.why: Correct answer: soap breaks the surface tension of the milk and reacts with the fat, which sets the colours moving. The water is the medium in which the colours float.

mcqs.q: The dance of colours shows:
options: A combination of physical and chemical changes
mcqs.why: Correct answer: it is a combination — breaking the surface tension is a physical process, and the soap reacting with the fat in the milk is a chemical process.

mcqs.q: Ghee made from vegetable oil is an example of a useful:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: changing oil into ghee by hydrogenation is a chemical change — hydrogen joins the oil (with a nickel catalyst) and a new substance, saturated fat, is formed.

lessons.title: Conduction, Convection and Radiation
lessons.notes_html:
Three Methods of Heat Transfer

MethodHow heat travelsNeeds a medium?
ConductionMolecules vibrate in their fixed places and pass heat to the neighbouring molecule — takes place only in solidsYes (solid)
ConvectionThe heated liquid or gas itself moves and carries heat (currents)Yes (liquid or gas)
RadiationHeat travels in the form of waves, even through a vacuumNo

Key Words

  • Temperature — the degree of hotness or coldness of a body.
  • Good conductor — a material that lets heat pass easily, e.g. copper.
  • Insulators — materials that never conduct heat: wood, plastic, cloth and cork. They block heat.

Why Conduction Happens Only in Solids

In conduction the molecules vibrate in their fixed places and pass heat to the next molecule. The molecules of solids are in fixed places, while the molecules of liquids and gases move about freely — so in liquids and gases heat is transferred by convection instead.

How the Sun's Heat Reaches Us

Between the sun and the earth there is a vacuum — no matter or medium. Conduction and convection both need a material medium, so the sun's heat can reach the earth only by radiation, travelling as waves.

mcqs.q: The degree of hotness or coldness of a body is called its:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: temperature. In the book's matching exercise, 'the degree of hotness or coldness of a hot body' matches temperature.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a good conductor of heat?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: copper conducts heat well, so it is a good conductor. Wood, plastic and cork are insulators that block heat.

mcqs.q: The process of heat transfer in a vacuum is:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: radiation. Heat travelling by waves needs no material medium, so it is the only method that works through a vacuum.

mcqs.q: We get heat from the sun through the ______ method.
mcqs.why: Correct answer: radiation. Between the sun and the earth there is a vacuum, through which heat can only come in the form of waves.

mcqs.q: Insulators never ______ heat.
mcqs.why: Correct answer: insulators never conduct heat. Things such as wood, plastic, cloth and cork are insulators that block the flow of heat.

mcqs.q: Why does conduction of heat take place only in solids?
options: In conduction molecules vibrate in fixed places and pass heat to neighbours — only solid molecules are in fixed places
mcqs.why: Correct answer: conduction needs molecules in fixed places that vibrate and pass heat on. Liquids and gases have freely moving molecules, so in them heat travels by convection.

mcqs.q: Why does the sun's heat not reach the earth by conduction or convection?
options: There is a vacuum between the sun and the earth, and conduction and convection need a material medium
mcqs.why: Correct answer: there is no matter/medium in the vacuum between the sun and the earth. Conduction and convection need a medium; radiation does not, so heat arrives only by radiation.

mcqs.q: In convection, heat is carried by:
options: The movement of the heated liquid or gas itself (currents)
mcqs.why: Correct answer: in convection the heated fluid itself moves and carries the heat — as in ocean currents, where sea water carries heat from one place to another.

mcqs.q: Which material would make the best handle for a hot pan?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: wood is an insulator — it does not conduct heat, so the handle stays cool enough to hold. Copper, iron and steel are conductors.

mcqs.q: Heat transfer in a solid metal rod happens mainly by:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: conduction. The molecules of the solid vibrate in their fixed places and pass the heat along the rod, molecule to molecule.

lessons.title: Convection in Air and Water — Breezes and Ocean Currents
lessons.notes_html:
Convection in the Sea — Ocean Currents

The currents produced in the sea are called ocean currents. An ocean current is a convection method of heat transfer — the sea water carries heat from one place to another through currents.

Land Breeze

The cool air blowing from the land towards the sea in the evening is called a land breeze. In the evening the land cools quickly, so the air blows from the land towards the sea. (The opposite flow, from sea to land, is the sea breeze.) Land and sea breezes are convection currents in the air.

Remember the Matching

StatementMatch
Currents produced in the seaOcean currents
Process of heat transfer in a vacuumHeat travelling by waves (radiation)
A poor radiator of heatWhite colour

mcqs.q: The cool air blowing from the land towards the sea in the evening is called:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: land breeze. In the evening the land cools quickly, so the air blows from the land towards the sea.

mcqs.q: An ocean current is a ______ method of heat transfer.
mcqs.why: Correct answer: convection. The sea water itself moves and carries heat from one place to another through currents.

mcqs.q: The currents produced in the sea are called:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: ocean currents. They are the sea's convection currents, moving warm and cold water over long distances.

mcqs.q: In the evening, the land:
options: Cools quickly, so air blows from land to sea
Heats up faster than the sea
Becomes hotter than in the day
mcqs.why: Correct answer: in the evening the land cools quickly. The air over the land then blows towards the sea — the land breeze.

mcqs.q: Ocean currents carry heat by:
options: Moving water carrying heat from one place to another
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the water itself moves, carrying heat with it — the essence of convection, unlike conduction where molecules stay in fixed places.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an example of convection?
options: Heat from the sun reaching the earth
A metal spoon getting hot in tea at the handle end by vibration
Heat felt near a fire without touching
mcqs.why: Correct answer: ocean currents are convection. The sun's heat and the warmth felt near a fire travel by radiation; the spoon heats by conduction.

mcqs.q: A land breeze blows:
options: From the land towards the sea in the evening
From the sea towards the land in the evening
mcqs.why: Correct answer: from the land towards the sea in the evening, because the land cools quickly after sunset.

mcqs.q: Convection can take place in:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: liquids and gases, whose molecules move freely and carry heat as currents. In solids, heat travels by conduction; in a vacuum, only radiation works.

mcqs.q: White colour is a poor radiator of heat because it:
options: Absorbs little heat and radiates little heat
mcqs.why: Correct answer: white colour absorbs little heat and radiates little heat — that is why, in the matching exercise, white is the poor radiator of heat.

mcqs.q: Sea water carrying heat through currents shows that water transfers heat by:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: convection. Currents are the moving part of the fluid carrying heat — in the sea these are the ocean currents.

lessons.title: Heat Transfer in Daily Life — Thermos, Refrigerator and Colours
lessons.notes_html:
The Thermos Flask

A thermos keeps hot things hot and cold things cold for a long time. Its double-walled glass bottle, the vacuum in between, the silver coating and the stopper block all three methods of heat transfer:

  • The vacuum stops conduction and convection (no medium).
  • The silver coating reflects radiation back.
  • The stopper blocks heat escaping from the top.

The Refrigerator Uses All Three Methods

A refrigerator works on all three methods of heat transfer: the cold air inside carries heat by convection, the evaporator fins take heat by conduction, and heat leaves from the back by radiation.

Five Uses of Radiation in Daily Life

  • The sun's heat reaches the earth by waves.
  • Standing near a fire or a heater, heat is felt without touching it.
  • In light/white clothes less heat is felt in summer, because a light colour reflects heat back.
  • Blackening the bottom of a kettle makes it absorb more heat.
  • Petrol tankers are painted white or silver so they reflect the sun's heat back and keep the petrol from getting hot.

Project Result — Do All Colours Absorb Equal Heat?

Ice in boxes wrapped with different coloured papers was kept in sunlight: the ice in the black box melted first (black absorbs the most heat), then the red/yellow boxes, and the ice in the white box melted last (white absorbs little heat and reflects most of it back). So white colour is best for protecting ice from melting quickly.

mcqs.q: Why do we use a thermos in daily life?
options: It keeps hot things hot and cold things cold for a long time by blocking all three methods of heat transfer
It makes drinks hot by itself
mcqs.why: Correct answer: a thermos keeps things at their temperature for a long time. Its double walls, vacuum, silver coating and stopper block conduction, convection and radiation.

mcqs.q: The vacuum between the double walls of a thermos stops:
options: Conduction and convection, because there is no medium
mcqs.why: Correct answer: with no air/matter between the walls, heat cannot travel by conduction or convection. The silver coating then reflects radiation back.

mcqs.q: A refrigerator works on which method(s) of heat transfer?
options: All three — conduction, convection and radiation
mcqs.why: Correct answer: all three methods. The cold air inside carries heat by convection, the evaporator fins take heat by conduction, and heat leaves from the back by radiation.

mcqs.q: Standing near a fire, we feel heat without touching it. This is:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: radiation. The heat travels from the fire to us in the form of waves, without any medium being heated in between.

mcqs.q: In summer, light or white clothes feel cooler because:
options: A light colour reflects heat back and absorbs less heat
mcqs.why: Correct answer: light colours reflect the sun's heat back, so less heat is absorbed and we feel less hot — one of the daily-life uses of radiation in the book.

mcqs.q: Blackening the bottom of a kettle helps because:
options: A black bottom absorbs more heat, so water boils faster
mcqs.why: Correct answer: black surfaces absorb the most heat. A blackened kettle bottom takes in more heat from the stove, heating the water quickly.

mcqs.q: Petrol tankers are painted white or silver so that they:
options: Reflect the sun's heat back and keep the petrol from getting hot
Can be seen at night only
mcqs.why: Correct answer: white and silver reflect the sun's heat back, keeping the petrol cool and safe. Dark colours would absorb heat and heat the petrol.

mcqs.q: In the colours project, the ice melted first in the box wrapped in:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the black box. Black colour absorbs the most heat, so its ice melted first; the white box's ice melted last because white reflects most heat back.

mcqs.q: To protect ice from melting quickly, the best colour for the box is:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: white. White absorbs little heat and reflects most of it back, so ice in a white box melts the slowest — white is a poor absorber and poor radiator of heat.

mcqs.q: The silver coating inside a thermos works by:
options: Reflecting radiation back, stopping heat loss by radiation
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the silver coating reflects the heat waves (radiation) back into the flask, just as white/silver paint on a petrol tanker reflects the sun's heat away.

lessons.title: Refraction of Light, Its Laws and Refractive Index
lessons.notes_html:
What Is Refraction?

When light goes from one medium into another (for example, from glass into water or from air into water), its speed changes and it bends. This bending is called refraction of light.

The Laws of Refraction (Snell's Laws)

  • Law 1: The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.
  • Law 2: The ratio between the speed of light in a vacuum and the speed of light in a medium is always constant; this ratio is called the refractive index of that medium.

Refractive Index

Refractive index (n) = speed of light in a vacuum ÷ speed of light in the medium.

  • Water: n = 1.33 — light travels 1.33 times more slowly in water than in a vacuum.
  • Diamond: n = 2.42 — light travels 2.42 times more slowly in diamond than in a vacuum.

Real Depth and Apparent Depth

Real depthApparent depth
The actual depth at which an object lies in waterThe depth at which the object appears to lie

Because of refraction, an object under water appears higher up and shallower than its real position, so the apparent depth is less than the real depth. A pencil in water looks bent for the same reason.

mcqs.q: Refraction of light happens when:
options: Light goes from one medium into another and bends because its speed changes
Light is blocked by an object
mcqs.why: Correct answer: refraction is the bending of light when it passes from one medium into another and its speed changes — for example, a pencil looks bent in water.

mcqs.q: According to the first law of refraction, the incident ray, refracted ray and normal all lie in:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: they all lie in the same plane. This is the first of Snell's laws of refraction.

mcqs.q: The refractive index of a medium is the ratio of:
options: Speed of light in the medium to speed in water
Speed of light in a vacuum to speed of light in the medium
Angle of incidence to angle of reflection
mcqs.why: Correct answer: refractive index = speed of light in a vacuum ÷ speed of light in the medium, and this ratio is always constant for a medium (Snell's second law).

mcqs.q: The refractive index of water is 1.33. This means light travels in water:
options: 1.33 times faster than in a vacuum
At the same speed as in a vacuum
1.33 times more slowly than in a vacuum
mcqs.why: Correct answer: light travels 1.33 times more slowly in water than in a vacuum. That slowing is what bends the light at the surface.

mcqs.q: The refractive index of diamond is:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: 2.42. Light travels 2.42 times more slowly in diamond than in a vacuum — much slower than in water (1.33).

mcqs.q: Real depth is:
options: The depth at which an object appears to lie
The actual depth at which an object lies in water
mcqs.why: Correct answer: real depth is the actual depth of the object in the water. Apparent depth is how deep it appears to be.

mcqs.q: Because of refraction, an object under water appears:
options: Higher up and shallower than its real position
mcqs.why: Correct answer: it appears higher up and shallower than it really is, so the apparent depth is less than the real depth — a refraction effect.

mcqs.q: The laws of refraction are also called:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: Snell's laws. They state the same-plane rule and the constant ratio that defines the refractive index.

mcqs.q: When light goes from glass (denser) into water (rarer) in the book's diagram, the refracted ray bends:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: away from the normal. Going from a denser medium into a rarer medium, light speeds up and bends away from the normal line.

mcqs.q: A pencil placed in water looks bent because of:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: refraction. Light from the pencil bends as it leaves the water, so the pencil appears shifted/bent from its real position.

lessons.title: Total Internal Reflection — Prisms, Mirage and the Fish Eye View
lessons.notes_html:
Total Internal Reflection

When light travels from a denser medium into a rarer medium and strikes the boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle, it does not pass out — it reflects back inside the denser medium. This is total internal reflection.

  • Critical angle of water = 48.8° (from the book's table).
  • In a reflecting prism, light strikes at an angle greater than the critical angle, so it undergoes total internal reflection.

Uses and Examples

ExampleHow it works
BinocularsReflecting prisms inside use total internal reflection to turn the rays of light through up to 180° so we can see distant objects
PeriscopeAlso works with reflecting prisms on the same principle
MirageAn illusion in a desert or on a hot road (see below)
Fish eye viewA fish sees the world above through total internal reflection (see below)

Mirage

A mirage is an illusion seen in a desert or on a hot road. The layers of hot air have different densities, so light passing through them bends and undergoes total internal reflection, making the image of a distant object look as if water were standing there.

Fish Eye View

A fish inside the water sees the world above through total internal reflection. The sun, the moon, birds and other animals appear in a circle at the surface of the water, but because of total internal reflection they look different from their real shape and position.

mcqs.q: In a reflecting prism, light strikes the surface at an angle which is ______ than the critical angle.
mcqs.why: Correct answer: greater. Only when the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle does the light undergo total internal reflection inside the prism.

mcqs.q: The critical angle of water is:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: 48.8 degrees, according to the book's table. Light in water striking the surface at more than this angle is totally internally reflected.

mcqs.q: In binoculars, ______ prisms are used to see distant objects.
mcqs.why: Correct answer: reflecting prisms. They work on the principle of total internal reflection and turn the rays of light through up to 180 degrees.

mcqs.q: Total internal reflection takes place when light goes from:
options: A denser medium into a rarer medium with the angle of incidence greater than the critical angle
A rarer medium into a denser medium at any angle
mcqs.why: Correct answer: light must pass from a denser into a rarer medium and strike at an angle greater than the critical angle — then it reflects back inside instead of passing out.

mcqs.q: A mirage is:
options: An illusion caused by light bending and total internal reflection in layers of hot air
mcqs.why: Correct answer: a mirage is an illusion seen in a desert or on a hot road. Hot air layers have different densities, light bends and totally internally reflects, and a distant object looks as if water were standing there.

mcqs.q: In the fish eye view, the fish sees the world above:
options: In a circle at the water surface, changed in shape and position by total internal reflection
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the fish sees the sun, moon, birds and animals gathered in a circle at the surface, but total internal reflection makes them look different from their real shape and position.

mcqs.q: Which instrument works on total internal reflection, like binoculars?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the periscope. The book lists binoculars and the periscope as instruments using reflecting prisms and total internal reflection.

mcqs.q: For total internal reflection, the angle of incidence must be:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: greater than the critical angle. If it is smaller, the light refracts out of the medium instead of reflecting back inside.

mcqs.q: Reflecting prisms in binoculars turn the rays of light through up to:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: up to 180 degrees. The prisms totally internally reflect the light, turning it around so the image reaches the eye correctly.

mcqs.q: The shimmering 'water' seen on a hot road on a sunny day is actually:
options: A mirage — total internal reflection of light in hot air layers
mcqs.why: Correct answer: it is a mirage. Layers of hot air near the road have different densities, so light bends and undergoes total internal reflection, imitating a pool of water.

lessons.title: Dispersion of Light and Colours
lessons.notes_html:
Dispersion of Light

The process of light splitting up into its different colours is called dispersion of light. When white light passes through a prism, it splits into seven colours. The rainbow is dispersion in nature: the white light of the sun passes through the drops of water in the air after rain and splits into seven colours.

Primary and Secondary Colours

Primary coloursSecondary colours
Three colours: red, green and blueColours obtained by mixing two primary colours together in the correct proportions

Why a Body Looks Black

If a body absorbs all the colours of light, it reflects back no colour, so it appears black. In general, a body shows the colour it reflects.

Uses of Colours of Light (from the book)

  • At home — making rooms pleasant and choosing furniture colours.
  • At school — colours for classrooms and boards.
  • On roads — signals, drivers' instructions and warnings.
  • Colours on buildings.
  • Colours on alarms and on ambulance and fire-brigade vehicles.
  • Coloured indicators on devices (such as the Wi-Fi or internet signal light).

If These Processes Did Not Occur… (project thinking)

  • No refraction → estimates of the depth and position of things in water would be wrong.
  • No total internal reflection → binoculars and periscopes would not work, and mirages would not be seen.
  • No dispersion → no rainbow would form and no spectrum of colours would be obtained from a prism.

mcqs.q: The process of light splitting up into its different colours is called:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: dispersion of light. When white light passes through a prism, it splits into seven colours.

mcqs.q: White light passing through a prism splits into:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: seven colours. This splitting is dispersion, and the band of colours is the spectrum.

mcqs.q: If a body absorbs all the colours of light, it will appear ______ in colour.
mcqs.why: Correct answer: black. A body that absorbs all colours reflects back no colour, so it appears black.

mcqs.q: The three primary colours are:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: red, green and blue are the three primary colours of light. Secondary colours are made by mixing two primaries in the correct proportions.

mcqs.q: Secondary colours are obtained by:
options: Mixing two primary colours together in the correct proportions
mcqs.why: Correct answer: secondary colours are made by mixing two primary colours together in the correct proportions.

mcqs.q: A rainbow is an example of:
options: Dispersion of light — sunlight splitting into seven colours through water drops
mcqs.why: Correct answer: a rainbow is dispersion: after rain, the sun's white light passes through the drops of water in the air and splits into seven colours.

mcqs.q: A red object looks red because it:
options: Reflects red light to our eyes
mcqs.why: Correct answer: a body shows the colour it reflects. Just as a body absorbing all colours looks black, a body reflecting red light looks red.

mcqs.q: Which use of colours of light is given in the book?
options: Colours on road signals, drivers' instructions and warnings
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the book's uses include road signals, drivers' instructions and warnings — also colours at home, at school, on buildings, on alarm and emergency vehicles, and device indicators.

mcqs.q: Coloured indicator lights on devices (like a Wi-Fi signal light) are an example of:
options: A use of the colours of light given in the book
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the book lists coloured indicators on devices — such as the Wi-Fi or internet signal — among the uses of colours of light.

mcqs.q: If dispersion did not occur in nature, we would not see:
options: Rainbows, and no spectrum of colours from a prism
mcqs.why: Correct answer: without dispersion there would be no rainbow and no spectrum of colours from a prism, as the book's project explains.

lessons.title: Types of Waves, Wavelength, Pitch and Loudness
lessons.notes_html:
Two Types of Waves

Sound wavesLight waves
Longitudinal wavesTransverse waves

So sound and light together cover both types of waves: sound is longitudinal, light is transverse.

Wavelength and Its Symbol

The wavelength is shown by the Greek letter lambda (λ).

Pitch, Quality and Intensity

  • The pitch of a sound depends on its frequency — changing the frequency changes the pitch (as in the bottle xylophone project).
  • The quality of sound depends on the shape of the source producing the sound.
  • The intensity of sound depends on the amplitude of the sound waves — the greater the amplitude, the louder the sound.
  • Amplitude is measured in metres, but it is also measured in decibels (dB). The decibel is the unit linked with amplitude/loudness in this book.

mcqs.q: What are the types of sound and light waves?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: both types — sound waves are longitudinal and light waves are transverse, so together they cover both types of waves.

mcqs.q: Sound waves are ______ waves.
mcqs.why: Correct answer: sound waves are longitudinal waves. Light waves, by contrast, are transverse waves.

mcqs.q: By which symbol is the wavelength shown?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: λ — the Greek letter lambda is the symbol for wavelength.

mcqs.q: Decibel (dB) is the unit of measurement of which thing?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: amplitude. According to the book, amplitude is measured in metres, but it is also measured in decibels (dB) — the unit tied to the loudness of sound.

mcqs.q: The intensity (loudness) of sound depends on:
options: The amplitude of the sound waves — greater amplitude means a louder sound
The shape of the room only
mcqs.why: Correct answer: intensity depends on amplitude. The greater the amplitude of the sound waves, the louder the sound is.

mcqs.q: The quality of sound depends on:
options: The shape of the source producing the sound
mcqs.why: Correct answer: quality depends on the shape of the source producing the sound — that is why different instruments and bottles sound different even at the same pitch.

mcqs.q: The pitch of a sound depends on its:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: pitch depends on frequency. In the xylophone project, changing the amount of water changes the frequency, and so the pitch of each bottle's sound changes.

mcqs.q: Light waves are ______ waves.
mcqs.why: Correct answer: light waves are transverse waves, while sound waves are longitudinal — the key pairing in this chapter's first question.

mcqs.q: If the amplitude of a sound wave becomes greater, the sound becomes:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: louder, because the intensity of sound depends on the amplitude of its waves. Pitch, instead, depends on frequency.

mcqs.q: Which pairing is correct?
options: Intensity of sound — amplitude; quality of sound — shape of the source
mcqs.why: Correct answer: intensity depends on amplitude, and quality depends on the shape of the source. These two facts are asked directly in the book's exercise.

lessons.title: Hearing Ranges and the Speed of Sound
lessons.notes_html:
The Human Hearing Range

The human ear can hear sounds from 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Sounds of frequency that the ear cannot hear are outside this range.

Speed of Sound in Different Media (book's table)

MediumSpeed of sound
Air343 m/s
Water1433 m/s
Steel6100 m/s

So sound passes fastest through steel — fastest in solids, slower in liquids, and slowest in gases.

Hearing Ranges of Some Living Things (book's table)

Living thingHearing range
Human20 – 20,000 Hz
Bat2,000 – 110,000 Hz
Dolphin20 – 120,000 Hz
Cat45 – 64,000 Hz
Whale10 – 31,000 Hz
Dog67 – 45,000 Hz
Elephant16 – 20,000 Hz

Note: the 20–15,000 Hz range sometimes printed with this exercise is not given for any animal in the book's table, so it cannot be matched to a particular animal on the book's basis.

mcqs.q: Sounds of which frequency range can the human ear hear?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: 20–20,000 Hz. According to the book's table, this is the human hearing frequency range.

mcqs.q: Through which thing does sound pass fastest of all?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: steel — 6100 m/s, compared with 1433 m/s in water and 343 m/s in air. Sound travels fastest in solids.

mcqs.q: The speed of sound in air is:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: 343 m/s in air. In water it is 1433 m/s and in steel 6100 m/s, from the book's table.

mcqs.q: The hearing range 2,000–110,000 Hz belongs to the:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the bat. Bats hear very high frequencies — 2,000 to 110,000 Hz — far above the human range.

mcqs.q: The hearing range 20–120,000 Hz belongs to the:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the dolphin, whose hearing range in the book's table is 20–120,000 Hz — the widest upper limit in the table.

mcqs.q: The cat's hearing range is:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: 45–64,000 Hz. For comparison: dog 67–45,000 Hz, whale 10–31,000 Hz, human 20–20,000 Hz.

mcqs.q: Which animal in the table can hear the lowest frequency (down to 10 Hz)?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the whale, with a range of 10–31,000 Hz — it can hear sounds lower than the human lower limit of 20 Hz (the elephant goes down to 16 Hz).

mcqs.q: Sound travels slowest in:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: air (343 m/s). Sound is slowest in gases, faster in liquids (1433 m/s in water) and fastest in solids (6100 m/s in steel).

mcqs.q: A sound of 30,000 Hz would be heard by:
options: A dog and a cat, but not by a human
mcqs.why: Correct answer: a dog (up to 45,000 Hz) and a cat (up to 64,000 Hz) can hear 30,000 Hz, but the human range stops at 20,000 Hz, so we cannot hear it.

mcqs.q: The elephant's hearing range from the book's table is:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: 16–20,000 Hz. The elephant hears slightly lower sounds than humans (down to 16 Hz) but has the same upper limit of 20,000 Hz.

lessons.title: Uses of Sound and the Bottle Xylophone
lessons.notes_html:
Five Means Showing the Importance of Sound for Humans (from the book)

  • Communication — talking and messaging through mobile phones and telephones.
  • Safety and warning — the doorbell, the smoke-warning device, sirens and alarms.
  • Entertainment — radio and the music system.
  • Traffic and announcements — the horn, the azan (call), traffic sounds and announcements.
  • Helping devices — the car's parking sensor, which warns of obstacles through sound.

The Bottle Xylophone (Project)

Five bottles were filled with different amounts of water — I: 100 ml, II: 200 ml, III: 250 ml, IV: 350 ml, V: 400 ml — arranged in the order IV, II, V, I, III and struck with a spoon.

  • Each bottle gives a different sound.
  • Reason: the quality of sound depends on the shape of the source, and the pitch depends on the frequency.
  • Changing the amount of water and the shape of the bottle changes both the pitch and the quality of the sound.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a safety and warning use of sound?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: sirens and alarms (and the doorbell and smoke-warning device) warn us through sound — one of the five means of sound's importance in the book.

mcqs.q: Talking and messaging through mobile phones and telephones is sound used for:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: communication. Our daily conversation depends on sound reaching from one person to another through phones and telephones.

mcqs.q: The car's parking sensor helps the driver by:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the parking sensor warns of obstacles through sound — a helping device that uses sound, from the book's list.

mcqs.q: Radio and the music system are examples of sound used for:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: entertainment. The book's five means are communication, safety and warning, entertainment, traffic and announcements, and helping devices.

mcqs.q: The horn, the azan and announcements belong to which use of sound?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: traffic and announcements — sounds that guide traffic and inform people in public places.

mcqs.q: In the bottle xylophone, each bottle gives a different sound because:
options: Quality depends on the shape of the source and pitch depends on frequency, and both change with the water level and bottle shape
mcqs.why: Correct answer: changing the amount of water and the shape of the bottle changes the frequency (pitch) and the quality of the sound, so every bottle sounds different.

mcqs.q: The bottles in the xylophone project were struck with:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: a spoon. The five bottles (100–400 ml of water) were arranged in the order IV, II, V, I, III and struck with a spoon to hear their sounds.

mcqs.q: If the amount of water in a xylophone bottle is changed, mainly the ______ of its sound changes.
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the pitch changes, because pitch depends on frequency, and the water level changes the frequency of the bottle's sound.

mcqs.q: A smoke-warning device uses sound to:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: it warns people — safety and warning is one of the five means by which sound is important for humans, along with doorbells, sirens and alarms.

mcqs.q: Which list gives the book's five means of the importance of sound?
options: Communication, safety and warning, entertainment, traffic and announcements, helping devices
mcqs.why: Correct answer: communication; safety and warning; entertainment; traffic and announcements; and helping devices (like the parking sensor) — these are the five means given in the book.

lessons.title: Electric Current and Its Units
lessons.notes_html:
What Is Electric Current?

Electric current is the movement of free electrons. When electrons flow in one direction through a conductor, a flow of electric charges is produced — and that flow is called electric current. So what actually flows in an electric circuit is electric charges (electrons) — the electrons freed from the outer shell of the conductor.

Units to Remember

QuantityUnitSymbol
Electric currentAmpereA
Potential difference (voltage)VoltV
ResistanceOhmΩ

mcqs.q: Electric current is:
options: The movement of free electrons in one direction through a conductor
mcqs.why: Correct answer: electric current is the movement (flow) of free electrons. When electrons flow in one direction through a conductor, the flow of electric charges produced is the current.

mcqs.q: What is it that flows as electric current in an electric circuit?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: electric charges — the electrons freed from the outer shell of the conductor flow through the circuit, and this flow itself is the current.

mcqs.q: Electric current is measured in ______ units.
mcqs.why: Correct answer: amperes (A). Electric current is measured in amperes; volts measure potential difference and ohms measure resistance.

mcqs.q: The unit for measuring the potential difference is the:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: volt (V). The potential difference (voltage) across a part of a circuit is measured in volts.

mcqs.q: The ______ unit is used for measuring resistance.
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the ohm (Ω) is the unit of resistance — the opposition a conductor offers to the flow of current.

mcqs.q: The electrons that flow in a conductor come from:
options: The outer shell of the conductor's atoms
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the electrons freed from the outer shell of the conductor's atoms flow through the circuit. Their one-direction flow is the electric current.

mcqs.q: Which pairing is correct?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: resistance is measured in ohms (Ω). Current is measured in amperes and potential difference in volts — the three units of this chapter.

mcqs.q: For current to flow, the electrons must move:
options: In one direction through the conductor
mcqs.why: Correct answer: when electrons flow in ONE direction through a conductor, a flow of electric charges is produced, which is called electric current.

mcqs.q: The symbol Ω stands for the unit of:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: Ω (ohm) is the unit of resistance, just as A (ampere) is the unit of current and V (volt) is the unit of potential difference.

mcqs.q: A conductor allows current to pass because it has:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: a conductor has free electrons — freed from the outer shells of its atoms — which flow in one direction to form the electric current.

lessons.title: Series and Parallel Circuits
lessons.notes_html:
Series Circuit and Parallel Circuit

Series circuitParallel circuit
Only one single path for the currentMore than one path (branches) for the current
All parts are connected in one single lineEach device is on its own branch
The same current flows through the whole circuitEach device can be switched on or off separately
If one bulb fuses, the whole circuit stopsIf one branch is switched off (or a bulb fuses), current keeps flowing in the other branches

Where Each Circuit Is Used

  • In homes, kitchens, classrooms and workplaces, the parallel circuit is fitted — because it provides more than one path for the current and each device can be switched on or off separately.
  • Your classroom is a parallel circuit: every bulb and fan has its own switch, and if one bulb fuses the others keep glowing.

mcqs.q: An electric circuit in which there is only one single path for the current is called a:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: a series circuit. All its parts are connected in one single line, so there is only one path for the current to flow through.

mcqs.q: In homes and in the kitchen, the ______ type of circuit is fitted.
mcqs.why: Correct answer: a parallel circuit is fitted in homes and kitchens, because it gives more than one path for the current and each device can be switched on or off separately.

mcqs.q: In a series circuit, if one bulb fuses:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the whole circuit stops, because there is only one path for the current — a fused bulb breaks the only path.

mcqs.q: In a parallel circuit, if one branch is switched off:
options: Current keeps flowing in the other branches
mcqs.why: Correct answer: current keeps flowing in the other branches. Each branch is an independent path in a parallel circuit.

mcqs.q: The same amount of current flows through the whole circuit in a:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: series circuit. With only one path, the same current passes through every part connected in that line.

mcqs.q: Your classroom has a parallel circuit because:
options: Every bulb and fan can be switched separately, and if one bulb fuses the others keep glowing
There is only one path for current
mcqs.why: Correct answer: separate switches for each bulb and fan, and the others keep glowing when one fuses — these are the signs of a parallel circuit with more than one path.

mcqs.q: A parallel circuit has:
options: More than one path (branches) for the current
Only one path for the current
mcqs.why: Correct answer: a parallel circuit provides more than one path for the current, which is why devices can work independently of each other.

mcqs.q: Which is an advantage of the parallel circuit in a home?
options: Each device can be switched on or off separately
All lights must be on together
mcqs.why: Correct answer: each device can be switched separately — the reason homes, kitchens and workplaces use parallel circuits.

mcqs.q: In a series circuit, all the parts are connected:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: in one single line. That is why there is exactly one path for the current and the same current flows through the whole circuit.

mcqs.q: If the bulbs of a string of lights are in series and one fuses, the others will:
options: Also stop glowing, because the only path is broken
mcqs.why: Correct answer: they will also stop. In series there is only one path; a single fused bulb breaks the circuit for all of them — unlike a parallel circuit.

lessons.title: Electrical Accidents and Safety
lessons.notes_html:
Accidents That Electricity Can Cause

  • Electric shock and electrocution — when current passes through the body a shock is felt; a person can be injured or can even die.
  • Short circuit — when too much current passes through wires, the wires heat up and touch each other, which produces sparks and can start a fire.
  • Fire — hot wires and sparks can set nearby things on fire.

Ways of Using Electricity Safely

  • Do not put any metal thing into electric sockets.
  • Never tamper with an electric wire, and never pull it out of the power-house wire.
  • Do not touch running electric things with wet hands.
  • Do not plug more things than the limit into sockets.
  • Do not touch a person who has received an electric shock with your hands; move them away from the wire with a non-metal thing (such as wood or rope).

Safety Devices

Use safety devices: fuse, MCB, earth wire, three-pin plug and ELCB.

mcqs.q: When too much current passes through wires, they heat up, touch each other and produce sparks. This accident is called a:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: a short circuit. The heated wires touch, sparks are produced, and a fire can start — one of the three main electricity accidents in the book.

mcqs.q: Which of these is one of the three main accidents caused by electricity?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: electric shock and electrocution — when current passes through the body, a person can be injured or can even die. The other two are short circuit and fire.

mcqs.q: You should never touch running electric things with:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: wet hands. Water makes the body conduct current much more easily, so touching electric things with wet hands can give a dangerous shock.

mcqs.q: To rescue a person who has received an electric shock, you should:
options: Move them away from the wire with a non-metal thing such as wood or rope
Pull the wire with bare hands
mcqs.why: Correct answer: never touch the shocked person with your hands — you would be shocked too. Move them away from the wire using a non-conductor such as wood or rope.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a safety device for electricity?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: a fuse is a safety device. The book's list is: fuse, MCB, earth wire, three-pin plug and ELCB.

mcqs.q: Putting a metal thing into an electric socket is:
options: Dangerous — it must never be done
mcqs.why: Correct answer: it must never be done. Metal conducts current into the body and causes electric shock — the first rule in the book's safety list.

mcqs.q: Plugging more things than the limit into a socket can cause:
options: Overloading, heating of wires and possibly a short circuit or fire
mcqs.why: Correct answer: overloading draws too much current; wires heat up, may touch and spark (short circuit) and can set nearby things on fire.

mcqs.q: The earth wire, MCB and ELCB are all:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: they are safety devices, together with the fuse and the three-pin plug, used to protect people and homes from electrical accidents.

mcqs.q: Hot wires and sparks from electricity can cause:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: fire — hot wires and sparks can set nearby things on fire, which is the third main accident caused by electricity.

mcqs.q: Which safety rule is correct?
options: Never pull a wire out of the power-house wire and never tamper with an electric wire
Touch sockets with metal to test them
Use wet hands for a better grip
mcqs.why: Correct answer: never tamper with an electric wire and never pull it out of the power-house wire. All the other choices are the dangerous actions the book warns against.

lessons.title: The Big Bang and the Beginning of the Universe
lessons.notes_html:
The Big Bang Theory

The scientists' theory which explains the beginning (origin) of the universe is called the Big Bang. According to this theory:

  • The universe began about 13.7 billion years ago from a single point (not 10 billion years ago).
  • That point was extremely hot and dense and contained all the matter of the universe.
  • A huge explosion took place in that point, from which space, time and matter came into existence, and the universe began to expand.
  • The universe is still expanding; it was hot at the beginning and then kept cooling down.

The Two Big Proofs

  • The expansion of the universe every day.
  • The Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation (CMB) — the leftover echo of the Big Bang.

What Is the CMB?

The CMB is very weak microwave radiation which came out of the hot universe at the beginning and is still spread in every direction in space. CMB stands for Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation (not 'Cosmic Matter Blue Radiation'). In 1992, NASA sent the COBE (Cosmic Background Explorer) satellite into space, which gave information about the map of the CMB.

Numbers to Remember

One billion = 1000 million. One million has 6 zeros (1,000,000) and one billion has 9 zeros (1,000,000,000).

mcqs.q: The Big Bang theory explains the ______ of the universe.
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the Big Bang theory explains the beginning (origin) of the universe — it tells that the universe began from a single point.

mcqs.q: 'This universe came into existence about 10 billion years ago.' True or false?
options: False — it began about 13.7 billion years ago
mcqs.why: Correct answer: False. The universe came into existence about 13.7 billion years ago, when the extremely hot, dense single point exploded in the Big Bang.

mcqs.q: At the very beginning, the single point of the universe was:
options: Extremely hot and dense, containing all the matter of the universe
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the point was extremely hot and dense and contained all the matter of the universe. Its explosion created space, time and matter.

mcqs.q: What came into existence from the Big Bang explosion?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: space, time and matter all came into existence from the Big Bang, and from then on the universe began to expand.

mcqs.q: The universe today is:
options: Still expanding, and cooler than at the beginning
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the universe is still expanding, and it was hot at the beginning and then kept cooling down — both facts support the Big Bang theory.

mcqs.q: CMB stands for:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: CMB stands for Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation — the leftover echo of the Big Bang, spread in every direction in space.

mcqs.q: The CMB is important because it is:
options: The biggest proof in support of the Big Bang theory
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the CMB is the leftover echo of the Big Bang — very weak microwave radiation from the hot early universe — and it is the biggest proof supporting the theory.

mcqs.q: In 1992, NASA sent which satellite to study the CMB?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: COBE — the Cosmic Background Explorer — was sent by NASA in 1992 and gave information about the map of the CMB. (True/False item in the book: True.)

mcqs.q: How many millions are there in one billion?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: 1000 million make one billion. One million has 6 zeros (1,000,000) and one billion has 9 zeros (1,000,000,000).

mcqs.q: Which are the two big proofs of the Big Bang theory?
options: The expansion of the universe and the Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation
mcqs.why: Correct answer: (1) the universe is expanding every day, and (2) the CMB — the leftover echo of the Big Bang — is still spread in every direction in space.

lessons.title: Stars — What They Are Made Of and Why They Shine
lessons.notes_html:
What Stars Are Made Of

Stars are actually big round balls of gas, which mainly contain hydrogen and helium.

Colour Shows Temperature

  • Blue stars are the hottest of all — their temperature is higher than that of red, yellow or orange stars.
  • Red stars are the least hot.
  • The Sun's temperature is about 6000°C.
  • Arcturus is an orange-coloured star with a temperature of 4000°C — it is NOT the hottest star; white and blue stars are hotter.

What Does a Star's Brightness Depend On?

  • The star's temperature — a hotter star shines more.
  • The star's size — a bigger star shines more.
  • The star's distance from the Earth — a nearer star looks brighter.
  • The matter in between — dust and gas between the star and the Earth reduce the light and lessen the brightness.

mcqs.q: Stars are big round balls of gas which mainly contain ______ and ______.
mcqs.why: Correct answer: hydrogen and helium. These two light gases make up almost all of a star (a nebula, for example, is 97% hydrogen and 3% helium).

mcqs.q: The temperature of blue-coloured stars is ______ than that of red, yellow or orange stars.
mcqs.why: Correct answer: higher. Blue stars are the hottest of all, and red stars are the least hot — colour is a guide to a star's temperature.

mcqs.q: 'The temperature of the Sun is about 6000 degrees Celsius.' True or false?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: True. According to the book's table, the temperature of the Sun is 6000°C.

mcqs.q: 'The star named Arcturus is the hottest of all stars.' True or false?
options: True, because it is the biggest
False — Arcturus is an orange star of 4000°C; white and blue stars are hotter
mcqs.why: Correct answer: False. Arcturus is an orange-coloured star with a temperature of 4000°C. White and blue stars are hotter than it.

mcqs.q: The brightness of a star depends on:
options: Its temperature, its size, its distance from Earth, and the matter in between
mcqs.why: Correct answer: four things — a hotter star shines more, a bigger star shines more, a nearer star looks brighter, and dust and gas in between reduce the light.

mcqs.q: A nearer star looks brighter mainly because of its:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: distance is one of the four factors of brightness. A nearer star looks brighter than a similar star that is far away.

mcqs.q: Dust and gas between a star and the Earth make the star look:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: less bright. The matter in between reduces the light coming from the star and lessens its brightness.

mcqs.q: Which star colour shows the highest temperature?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: blue stars are the hottest of all; red stars are the least hot, with orange and yellow in between.

mcqs.q: A star that is both hotter and bigger will generally shine:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: more — both temperature and size increase brightness, together with distance and the matter in between.

mcqs.q: The two main gases in a star are the same two that fill a star-forming nebula in the ratio:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: a nebula contains 97 percent hydrogen and 3 percent helium — the gases from which stars form, and of which stars are mainly made.

lessons.title: The Life of a Star — From Nebula to White Dwarf or Black Hole
lessons.notes_html:
The Life of a Low-Mass (Sun-like) Star

StageWhat happens
1. NebulaA cloud of gas and dust (97% hydrogen, 3% helium)
2. Proto-star phaseUnder gravity the cloud shrinks and becomes a hot ball
3. Main sequence phaseThe longest and stable phase — hydrogen burns and becomes helium
4. Red giant phaseWhen the hydrogen finishes, the star swells into a very big red ball
5. Planetary nebula phaseThe star throws off its outer matter
6. White dwarfAt the end, the centre is left as a small, dense, white body

Black Holes

A black hole is a place in space where matter collapses onto itself and even light cannot escape from it, because its gravity is so strong.

  • Only a very massive big star ends as a black hole: after a supernova explosion, its remaining matter collapses onto itself.
  • A Sun-like star does NOT end as a black hole — it finally becomes a white dwarf.

mcqs.q: A black hole is a place in space where ______ collapses onto itself and even ______ cannot escape.
mcqs.why: Correct answer: matter collapses onto itself and its gravity becomes so strong that even light cannot escape — that is a black hole.

mcqs.q: What type of star ends up as a black hole at the end of its life?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: a very massive big star. When such a star ends with a supernova explosion, its remaining matter collapses onto itself and becomes a black hole.

mcqs.q: 'The last stage of the life of a Sun-like star is a black hole.' True or false?
options: False — a Sun-like star finally becomes a white dwarf
mcqs.why: Correct answer: False. A Sun-like (low-mass) star ends as a white dwarf; a black hole forms only from very massive stars with much more matter.

mcqs.q: The first stage in the life of a star is the:
options: Nebula — a cloud of gas and dust
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the nebula. A star begins as a cloud of gas and dust containing 97% hydrogen and 3% helium, which gravity pulls together.

mcqs.q: In the proto-star phase:
options: The star throws off its outer matter
Under gravity the cloud shrinks and becomes a hot ball
The star becomes a white dwarf
mcqs.why: Correct answer: in the proto-star phase the nebula shrinks under the force of gravity and becomes a hot ball — the young star.

mcqs.q: The main sequence phase is:
options: The longest and stable phase, in which hydrogen burns and becomes helium
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the main sequence is the longest and stable phase of a star's life, in which hydrogen burns and becomes helium — our Sun is in this phase.

mcqs.q: When the hydrogen of a Sun-like star finishes, it becomes a:
options: Red giant — it swells into a very big red ball
mcqs.why: Correct answer: a red giant. With its hydrogen finished, the star swells and becomes a very big red ball, before throwing off its outer matter as a planetary nebula.

mcqs.q: In the planetary nebula phase, the star:
options: Throws off its outer matter and takes the shape of a planetary nebula
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the star throws off its outer matter, leaving the hot centre that finally remains as a white dwarf.

mcqs.q: A white dwarf is:
options: The small, dense, white body left at the centre at the end of a Sun-like star's life
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the white dwarf is the final stage of a low-mass (Sun-like) star — a small, dense, white body left after the planetary nebula phase.

mcqs.q: A very big star ends its life with which event before becoming a black hole?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: a supernova explosion. After it, the remaining matter of the very massive star collapses onto itself and becomes a black hole.

lessons.title: Galaxies and the Hubble Sequence
lessons.notes_html:
What Is a Galaxy?

A galaxy is a huge combined collection of stars, gas and dust, held together by the force of gravity.

Types of Galaxies (the Hubble Sequence)

The classification of galaxies was presented by Edwin Hubble in 1920 and is called the Hubble sequence (it was not Einstein's idea).

TypeShape and features
SpiralSeveral spiral-like arms and a bright centre; our Milky Way is spiral
EllipticalOval (egg-like) in shape; mostly contain old stars
LenticularLens-shaped; has a disc like a spiral galaxy but no spiral arms — an in-between type of spiral and elliptical galaxies
IrregularNo fixed shape

The book also mentions starburst galaxies, merging galaxies, active galaxies and radio galaxies.

Our Milky Way

  • The galaxy in which the Earth (and the Sun) is present is the Milky Way.
  • Our Sun is located about 25,000 light years from the centre of the galaxy (not 15,000).

mcqs.q: A galaxy is a huge combined collection of ______, ______ and ______.
mcqs.why: Correct answer: stars, gas and dust, held together by the force of gravity — that is what makes a galaxy.

mcqs.q: The lenticular galaxy is an in-between type of ______ and ______ galaxies in shape.
mcqs.why: Correct answer: spiral and elliptical. A lenticular galaxy has a disc like a spiral galaxy but no spiral arms, and it also looks like an elliptical galaxy.

mcqs.q: The name of the galaxy in which the Earth is present is:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the Milky Way. Our Sun and Earth are present in the Milky Way galaxy, which is a spiral galaxy. (True/False item in the book: True.)

mcqs.q: 'The scientist Einstein presented the idea of the classification of galaxies.' True or false?
options: False — Edwin Hubble presented it in 1920; it is called the Hubble sequence
mcqs.why: Correct answer: False. The classification of galaxies was presented by Edwin Hubble in 1920 and is called the Hubble sequence.

mcqs.q: Our Sun is located about how far from the centre of the Milky Way?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: about 25,000 light years, according to the book — the statement '15,000 light years' is false.

mcqs.q: Spiral galaxies have:
options: Several spiral-like arms and a bright centre in the middle
Only old stars and an egg shape
mcqs.why: Correct answer: spiral galaxies have spiral-like structures or arms with a bright centre — our Milky Way is also a spiral galaxy.

mcqs.q: Elliptical galaxies are:
options: Oval (egg-like) in shape and mostly contain old stars
mcqs.why: Correct answer: elliptical galaxies are oval (egg-like) in shape and mostly contain old stars, as described in the Hubble sequence.

mcqs.q: A galaxy with no fixed shape is called:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: irregular galaxies have no fixed shape. The four main Hubble types are spiral, elliptical, lenticular and irregular.

mcqs.q: Besides the four main types, the book also mentions:
options: Starburst, merging, active and radio galaxies
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the book also mentions starburst galaxies, merging galaxies, active galaxies and radio galaxies, besides spiral, elliptical, lenticular and irregular.

mcqs.q: Lenticular galaxies differ from spiral galaxies because they:
options: Have a disc but no spiral arms
mcqs.why: Correct answer: lenticular (lens-shaped) galaxies have a disc like spiral galaxies but no spiral arms — that is why they are an in-between type.

lessons.title: Telescopes, Light Years, Parallax and Constellations
lessons.notes_html:
The Telescope

The telescope is the instrument which can collect the light coming from faraway things (heavenly bodies) and form their image.

What Is a Light Year?

A light year is a unit for measuring distance — the distance that light covers in one year is called one light year. (It measures distance, not time!)

Measuring the Distance of Nearby Stars — Parallax

  • A nearby star is observed from two opposite places of the Earth's orbit, with a gap of six months.
  • On both occasions the star appears slightly shifted against the background of the faraway stars; this apparent change is called parallax.
  • From the measurement of the parallax, the distance of the star from the Earth is found, stated in light years.

Constellations and Asterisms

A constellation is a group of stars which, seen from the Earth, shows the pattern or shape of something. That shape is only apparent (imaginary), because those stars are not actually close to one another. Note: the book does not give a definition of the word 'asterism' in this chapter's text — it only explains the constellation.

mcqs.q: The telescope is the instrument which can collect the ______ coming from faraway things.
mcqs.why: Correct answer: light. A telescope collects the light coming from faraway heavenly bodies and forms their image.

mcqs.q: A light year is a unit for measuring:
options: Distance — the distance light covers in one year
mcqs.why: Correct answer: distance. One light year is the distance that light covers in one year; star distances (like the Sun's 25,000 light years from the galactic centre) are stated in light years.

mcqs.q: The distance of nearby stars is measured by which method?
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the parallax method. The star is observed from two opposite points of Earth's orbit six months apart, and its apparent shift gives its distance.

mcqs.q: In the parallax method, the same star is observed again after a gap of:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: six months — the time Earth takes to reach the opposite side of its orbit, giving the widest base for observing the star's shift.

mcqs.q: The apparent shift of a nearby star against the background of faraway stars is called:
mcqs.why: Correct answer: parallax. From the measurement of this apparent change, the distance of the star from the Earth is found out.

mcqs.q: 'Constellations in the sky only reflect an imaginary body.' True or false?
options: False — stars in a constellation touch each other
True — the pattern is only apparent; the stars are not actually close to one another
mcqs.why: Correct answer: True. A constellation is a group of stars that appears to show a shape from Earth, but that shape is only apparent because the stars are far apart in space.

mcqs.q: A constellation is:
options: A group of stars which, seen from Earth, shows the pattern or shape of something
mcqs.why: Correct answer: a constellation is a group of stars showing an apparent pattern or shape of something when seen from the Earth.

mcqs.q: Why must star distances be stated in light years and not in kilometres?
options: The distances are so huge that a large unit is needed — one light year is the distance light covers in a whole year
mcqs.why: Correct answer: star distances are enormous (the Sun alone is 25,000 light years from the galactic centre), so the light year — the distance light covers in one year — is the practical unit.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the word 'asterism' is correct according to the book?
options: It is fully defined in the chapter
It is another name for a galaxy
Its definition is not given in this chapter's text; the book only tells about constellations
It is a type of telescope
mcqs.why: Correct answer: the definition of an asterism is not given in the text of this chapter, so it cannot be answered from the book. The book only explains the constellation.

mcqs.q: The background stars used in parallax measurement are:
options: Faraway stars, against which the nearby star appears to shift
mcqs.why: Correct answer: faraway stars form the background. The nearby star appears slightly shifted against them when seen from opposite sides of Earth's orbit — that shift is the parallax.
